8 Essentials for Your Family's First Trip to Disney World

📅 03 Jan 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Moms

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that katie Leigh Matthews is a contributing writer for Moms.com.
  • She’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years.
  • She loves that through Moms.com, she can put her chronic overthinking of every parenting decision to good use by saving readers time and hopefully a headache or two.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that katie Leigh Matthews is a contributing writer for Moms.com. As the mom of a sweet and sensitive 9-year-old boy and a wild and free 5-year-old girl, she brings her ever-evolving experience of parenting to everything she writes.

She’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years. With a degree in communications and a fascination for all things mental health, she seeks to uncover and share what genuinely helps us be more of who we are capable of being, especially with our kids. Towards that end, she writes often on introversion and the trait of high sensitivity to highlight their strengths and promote more self-compassion among all who share them. She regularly collaborates with experts in these fields to create content that informs, encourages, and empowers.

She loves that through Moms.com, she can put her chronic overthinking of every parenting decision to good use by saving readers time and hopefully a headache or two.

Sources indicate that katie lives in Birmingham, Alabama, with her husband and two kids. On any given day she’s probably either rewatching her favorite shows for the 100th time or dipping her toes in any creek she can find.

It has been revealed that you’ve booked your tickets. You’ve planned your itinerary. You’ve figured out the My Disney Experience App (you think.) You’re as ready as you can be for your family’s first trip to Disney World. Then it dawns on you: What do you need to pack? Shopping for essentials for your first family trip to Disney World is an art – it’s about knowing your family and what you all need to thrive on one of the most exciting, most magical, and yes, sometimes stressful family vacations.

Industry observers note that A little online searching will quickly convince you you'll need to buy extra luggage just to pack park essentials, but don’t stress. As an easily-overwhelmed mom who recently braved Disney World for the first time, I've got some hard-won advice to help guide your vacation prep and inform your packing list. Plus, I've scoured the internet for top picks of the most-used sanity-saving products to make the happiest place on earth live up to its name for you and your family.

Recent findings suggest that for many parents, taking the kids to Disney World at least once during their childhood is a bucket list goal. When that dream is finally realized, there is a mix of idyllic anticipation and anxious uncertainty. It’s not surprising that many parents find planning for a trip to Disney World to be a stressful experience.

In a recent development, when it comes to Disney World, there are two types of parents: those who have fond memories of their own childhood Disney vacation, and those who hope to give their own kids the trip they didn’t get to experience growing up. Whichever type you are, the goal is the same: To give your kids a core-memory-making family vacation they’ll cherish forever. Of course, a love of Disney also evokes childhood nostalgia that is so fun to share with your own children. The legacy of classic and modern Disney characters, movies, and parks is a special thing to pass on to the next generation and something that carries a lot of weight for many.

Sources indicate that along with all the hopes and expectations wrapped up in a family trip to Disney World, the cost of the vacation only adds to the pressure to make it the best trip ever. For budget travelers, the average weeklong Disney World vacation for a family of four can cost $6,000 or more, according to NerdWallet, so ensuring you get your money’s worth is a huge factor. Not only that, but with so much to see, do, and experience in the parks, a vacation to Disney World is a complex trip to blueprint. Some families even turn to Disney vacation planners and travel agents to help with the sheer volume of logistical planning involved.

As tempting as it may be, you don’t need to add-to-cart every single item you see on ‘Must Have Disney Essentials’ lists. Before you start shopping, it pays to think through what will help your family enjoy your trip the most. The best travel products for families will vary, so evaluate these factors before you start shopping:.

Recent findings suggest that of course, start with the makeup of your family. How old will your kids be on the trip, and what needs and preferences correspond with their ages? Strollers are a significant decision for many, and there are lots of pros and cons to consider: Will it help or hurt to have a stroller for airports? Is it worth it to lug a stroller to the parks? Would renting Disney World strollers be a better option? The answer will be different for every family, so don’t listen to advice that insists on a right answer. Our youngest was six on our trip and I seriously considered taking or renting a stroller. She ended up walking the parks like a champ and I was glad we didn’t have to deal with a stroller! Had she been a year younger, though, I am sure a stroller would have been our saving grace.

What are your kids most looking forward to in the parks? How will they handle long lines? Will you need to anticipate an afternoon nap each day? Should you stock up on a few fun toys ahead of time so your kiddos aren’t pining for the theme park loot, or do you just need to upgrade your child’s luggage? A Disney World vacation will look very different depending on the ages of your kids, so narrow your list of essentials based on them.

Sources indicate that A surefire way to preemptively ruin your first trip to Disney World is to forget your own needs in the process. For parents, Disney World is fun, sure, but there’s also a lot of planning, incessant crowds, unrelenting heat, not to mention the never-ending soundboard of the kids' needs and wants. Take a moment and think about what essentials you need to make the most of the trip, and perhaps even a few indulgent spa day gifts to help melt stress away at the end of a non-stop Disney World day.

A travel-size umbrella that offers heavy-duty weather protection.

Sources indicate that weather is a major factor in whether Disney World lives up to being “the happiest place on earth.” You likely know to expect warmer temperatures year-round, and extreme heat in the summer. But surprise rain showers are also a common occurrence in Orlando. Luckily, the Repel Compact Umbrella can help on both fronts. Not only will you be happy you have it if you get caught in a shower, but it will also filter UV rays when the sun is beating down. In fact, Repel even offers a UPF 50+ UV protection version of the umbrella to block out 99% of UV rays.

It has been revealed that the umbrella's double-vented canopy is designed to withstand winds up to 85 MPH, so you won’t have to worry about it inverting. It is a heavy-duty umbrella packed into a compact travel size, opens and collapses with a push of a button, and is definitely worth tossing in your park bag. Reviewers say it performs as advertised – one even mentioned the umbrella “loves wind” – with just a few saying the only issue they’ve had is closing it. (And yes, Disney World does allow umbrellas!).

This microfiber towel will save the day in all sorts of ways when you’re out and about, and packs into its own travel bag.

When you’re at the parks from sun up to sun down, unexpected needs are bound to arise, and the Rainleaf Microfiber Towel will be a lifesaver for many of them. Kid drop Dole Whip down their shirt? Want to dry off a wet seat? Need to add more sun shade to the stroller? Chances are you’ll be reaching for this towel all day long. Not only is it compact and made for travel, but it also absorbs five times its own weight and dries incredibly fast. If it’s super hot, drench the towel in cold water to help you cool off, then drape it over your backpack or stroller as you walk around to let it air dry.

Running from $9 to $20 a piece, depending on the size, it’s worth giving each family member their own, or grabbing a few to designate for certain purposes – one for clean up, one for shade and sweat, and one as a picnic blanket for parades or just a quick rest.

This compact travel charger keeps your devices topped up all day long.

Sources indicate that between taking a million pictures and using the Disney app to do everything from making meal orders and reservations to finding the next ride (or nearest restroom!), you’ll be using your phone a lot in the parks. The Anker Portable Charger ensures your devices stay charged up all day long. It has a universal USB-C cable and delivers 10,000mAh (milliamp hours), delivering the equivalent of two full smartphone charges. At 30W charging speed, you can expect it to fully charge a phone in about an hour – which is how long you’ll be lining for some rides anyway.

According to recent reports, the charger is just a tad bigger than a credit card, and weighs about as much as a phone. It can charge three devices at once (you just need extra charging cables) and the cable connector stores in the battery pack for safekeeping between uses. Coming in under $30, it’s well worth the peace of mind so you don’t miss a single picture-perfect moment, even as the last firework illuminates the night sky.

One tip I got from a Disney World cast member is to take screenshots of the QR codes, order confirmations, lightning lane arrival windows, and anything else you may need for reference from the My Disney Experience App so you aren’t constantly having to access the app, which can drain your phone battery.

Take a rest whenever you need to with this super practical compact folding stool.

Recent findings suggest that the Boreeman Folding Stool is as close as it gets to realizing the idea of pants that turn into a chair, but arguably way more practical. If your back just isn’t what it used to be, or you’ve got a kiddo who you know will complain about standing in line, this folding stool will single-handedly save your Disney World trip. The collapsible seat locks into place at various heights up to 17.72 inches. It packs down into a disc that is 9.84 inches by 2.36 inches with a carrying strap for added convenience. Use it in ride lines, waiting for parades or demonstrates, or just whenever you need to take a load off. It also comes in handy to help little ones with bathroom needs.

It has been revealed that the stool is highly rated with 4.4 stars from over 8,000 reviewers, but some say it’s not super comfortable, while others warn theirs broke while sitting on it. Still, other reviewers say they still use theirs often over a year later. It comes in tons of fun colors and can slide into bags, backpacks, or stroller compartments. It’s also light enough at 2.5 pounds for many kids to carry it through a ride line themselves.

Make any moment magical with these Disney-themed bubble wands.

The struggle to not buy every cute thing you see in Disney World is real, and the Little Kids Disney Light and Sound Musical Bubble Wand is here to help. Light-up bubble wands are all the rage in the parks, and they come with a hefty price tag. If you’re looking to save money where you can on your trip, surprise your little one with a pre-bought bubble wand for a fraction of the cost of the park varieties, which cost upwards of $35.

These wands are themed with all their favorite characters, including Mickey Mouse, Tiana, Elsa, Moana, and more. They light up, play music, and come with extra bubbles so your kiddo can join in the bubble wand fun all day long. Some reviewers were not satisfied with the durability and quality of the wand, while others say it was perfect for their Disney Parks trip.

Outsmart unpredictable weather with this family pack of reusable ponchos.

It has been revealed that my family didn’t end up needing the Lingito Rain Ponchos Family Pack for rain, but we were so glad we used them on Tiana’s Bayou Adventure! We got in one of the first virtual queue time slots of the morning, and without the ponchos, we would have been utterly soaked for the rest of the day. This family pack gets the job done at keeping your family (and your backpacks) dry, whether the water is weather or ride-related. The adult ponchos have drawstrings, and while I understand they might pose a hazard for kids, I wish the kid ponchos could tighten for a better fit. My kids held theirs closed just under their chins when we dropped down the log flume.

Sources indicate that they come compactly packed in small disposable bags, and you’ll be hard-pressed to fold them back in after you open them. The Amazon listing describes these ponchos as both reusable and disposable, which is accurate. While they can be dried out and used again on a trip, they might be too much trouble to save for your next adventure (however, one reviewer reports their family has used their set again and again). Still, at $10 for a pack of four (two adult and two kid-sized ponchos), they are well worth throwing in your bag every day in case you get caught in one of those notorious surprise Orlando rain showers – or just so you stay dry on wet rides.

This wearable fan rests around your neck for hands-free cooling wherever you go.

If you're worried about the relentless Orlando heat more than any other part of your Disney trip, do yourself a favor and pack the FrSara Portable Neck Fan. It’s encased blade vents blow air all the way around the back of the neck and out the ends to keep you noticeably cooler without having to worry about hazards like tangling hair. With a noise level of 25 dB – the equivalent of the ambient noise of a ‘silent’ PC – you can even keep it running indoors through those winding ride lines without being a nuisance to yourself or others …though it’s worth noting that some reviewers find it too loud.

The fan's working time ranges from four to 16 hours, and its USB-C charging port means you can recharge on the go with a portable device charger. With three speeds and 360-degree surround airflow, it might not quite make you forget you’re in Orlando, but it can certainly take the edge off the heat.

This lightweight travel stroller folds down easily and has four recline positions with tons of storage.

To pack a stroller or not to pack a stroller, that is the question for families making the pilgrimage to Disney World. If you decide to bring your own, the Summer Infant 3Dlite Stroller is our pick for Disney World for a few reasons. First, the stroller complies with Disney World’s list of prohibited items regarding stroller size, and reviewers do confirm that they used this stroller in Disney World. Second, the price is right at under $100, though it’s worth noting that single-stroller rentals at Disney World go for $15 per day, and $13 per day for multi-day rentals.

Industry observers note that the stroller is lightweight, has four recline positions for napping on the go, a pop out weather canopy, and tons of extra storage, including a cup holder, close-top bag, and large storage compartment underneath the seat. Reiewers agree that this is a great, budget-friendly stroller for travel, and is highly rated at 4.6 stars with over 7,000 reviews. Plus, it has a weight capacity of 50 pounds, which is on the upper end for most travel strollers. So if you have an older kid who might not be able to last the entire day on foot, this stroller can be a lifesaver.

Industry observers note that take it from me, even anxious, stressed-out parents can make the most of their family’s first trip to Disney World. Resolve to manage your stress level by taking good care of yourself, setting yourself up for success by planning based on what will make it magical for your family, and packing essentials that will help everyone enjoy the trip.

The key is managing expectations, especially your own. Knowing that a vacation with kids is still parenting, just in a different location – and understanding that parenting in Disney World isn’t always a walk in the park – can help you make this trip every bit as magical for your kiddos as you hoped, though it likely won’t feel like it to you. So make sure you stop and take in their sweet faces when they meet their favorite characters, when they go on the ride they were so excited for, and as they watch as fireworks illuminate the night. You’ll experience the magic, guaranteed!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that will it take a zombie apocalypse to fix masculinity?
  • I won’t spoil too much in the way of the plot but I will say that the way the story speaks to masculinity — wading through lost men, toxic lies, and not-so-symbolic alpha males (in the form of one truly terrifying zombie) — is thoughtful and fresh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Danny Boyle’s zombie trilogy is a timely and important meditation about masculinity.

Recent findings suggest that will it take a zombie apocalypse to fix masculinity? The thought occurred to me as I sat in a theater taking in Danny Boyle’s 28 Years Later the other day. This intense, gory, nudity-laden flick was also one of a surprisingly heartwarming journey for a young boy, Spike, who doesn’t buy into his community’s view of the world. Everyone around him is fearful, incurious, and readily accepts convenient and clear falsehoods about their lives. Spike seeks hope, even if it requires him to face the violent, cruel, and potentially fatal real world off his island.

I won’t spoil too much in the way of the plot but I will say that the way the story speaks to masculinity — wading through lost men, toxic lies, and not-so-symbolic alpha males (in the form of one truly terrifying zombie) — is thoughtful and fresh. In context of the cultural landscape for boys and men today, it’s the kind of exploration we could really use.

Two months ago, Scott Galloway, a professor of marketing at NYU and media tour de force affectionately known on his podcast as Prof G, took to The View to talk, as he does so often, about masculinity.

In a recent development, “I like the idea of restoring an aspirational vision of masculinity,” he said to a room that seemed, a bit surprisingly, in total agreement. “I don’t think there’s anything wrong with leaning into your femininity or masculinity if it feels natural.”.

In his view, this vision of masculinity involves three pillars: provider, procreator, and protector.

In 28 Years Later, Spike becomes the provider, chasing the health care his mom needs that his dad ignores.

When it comes to the provider, “every man at the outset of his career should take economic responsibility for his household. Sometimes that means getting out of the way” of your more successful partner, he says, and other times it means stepping up. For procreation, he says we should channel “that fire of desire… the right ways [to] make you a better man — kinder, stronger, thinking about how you dress … showering, for God’s sake.”.

Sources indicate that finally, he indicates that in an aspirational vision of masculinity, “your default operating system is protection.” This is a more gentle and empathetic pillar than it might sound on its face. “A lot of women don’t feel safe on the subway,” he explains, “or they see men walking down the street, they cross the sidewalk.” This is due to men eschewing their duty as protector. And “it’s not just physical,” he continues. “When you see a group being demonized, your default setting as a man is you move to protection.”.

In 28 Years Later, Spike found himself chasing this view of masculinity headlong: providing the health care his mom needed that his dad would not, protecting her from zombies and himself from indoctrination, not exactly chasing procreation (he’s 12) but rejecting his father’s philandering example. The fact that he lives in a post-apocalyptic landscape in many senses brings clarity to his vision. When there are no worldly comforts, moral clarity arises.

Danny Boyle and Prof G have this in common: They’re both speaking to the broadest possible audiences about things that so many men primarily discuss with, well, other men. With 28 Years Later raking in over $100 million at the box office already and The View’s audience being, well, The View’s audience, it’s refreshing to see such discussion spilling out into the public.

Sources indicate that masculinity is making a comeback. It’s time to talk about it.

How to Winterize Salvias – 5 Easy Ways to Protect Plants and Guarantee Dazzling Blooms Next Year

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a seasoned gardener, if you ask me to name an easy-to-grow flowering perennial that returns reliably year after year, salvia would be at the top of my list.
  • Sources indicate that yet, despite their tough and easygoing nature, winter is the one season where salvias do need a bit of care and attention.
  • Taking action now, in this narrow window between autumn's close and winter's first freeze, is critical.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a seasoned gardener, if you ask me to name an easy-to-grow flowering perennial that returns reliably year after year, salvia would be at the top of my list. In my own garden, my ‘Hot Lips’ shrubby salvia shrugs off summer drought, asks for very little maintenance, and blooms generously from late spring through to November. Their nectar-rich flower spikes are magnets for hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies, drenching borders in rich purples, electric blues, hot pinks, and velvety crimsons.

Sources indicate that yet, despite their tough and easygoing nature, winter is the one season where salvias do need a bit of care and attention. The genus Salvia is vast, encompassing over a thousand species of annuals, woody sub-shrubs, and herbaceous perennials from regions as diverse as cold alpine meadows, dry Mediterranean hillsides, and tropical cloud forests. Because their natural habitats differ dramatically, their winter cold tolerance does, too. What protects a hardy meadow sage in New England will not save a tender Mexican bush salvia during a sudden polar snap. So winter salvia care needs to be adapted accordingly.

Taking action now, in this narrow window between autumn's close and winter's first freeze, is critical. Winter damage can happen fast, and yet knowing how to winterize salvias is surprisingly easy. By understanding your variety's cold tolerance and taking action fast, you can help prime your salvia in winter. Here’s how to easily guide your garden favorites through to next spring, so you can enjoy their lush, vibrant blooms for years to come.

Sources indicate that the precise winter protection required will depend on where you live and the type of salvia you are growing. Some are cold-hardy perennials, while others are tender, frost-sensitive tropicals. So successful winterizing begins with identifying growth habit and hardiness classification. Deciduous herbaceous salvias like meadow sage (S. nemorosa cultivars like Caradonna and May Night) and woodland sage (S. pratensis) are cold-hardy in USDA hardiness zones 3-8. These perennials die back after hard frosts, resting safely underground before surging back in spring. They need little winter protection beyond good drainage and light insulation.

According to recent reports, shrubby, semi-hardy salvias (S. greggii and S. microphylla) occupy a middle ground, thriving in zones 6-9. These semi-evergreen sub-shrubs develop woody stems that can be damaged by sudden cold snaps or damp winter soils. In colder microclimates within these zones, they require protective mulching and shelter from wet winds. Finally, tender subtropical and tropical salvias, including velvet-flowered Amistad and Mexican bush sage (S. leucantha), flourish only in frost-free zones 8-11. These are large, bushy salvias that are killed by hard winter freezes, so in cooler zones, they require extra winter protection.

Before you begin, test your soil moisture levels and check that water drains away readily after rain. The XLUX Long Probe Deep Soil Moisture Meter, available from Amazon is a great dual soil moisture and pH diagnostic probe, giving instant readings to help you identify waterlogged soil pockets before the ground freezes. Once your soil is identified, you’re ready to take action. Here we clarify when to cut your salvias back, how to protect the roots from cold and wet conditions, and how to ensure you see your jewel-toned flowering favorites again next year.

According to recent reports, when salvias start looking ragged, the natural impulse is to reach for the bypass pruners and shear everything back to a tidy clump. This could be the most damaging mistake you make. Many perennial salvias (especially semi-woody and herbaceous varieties) have hollow, straw-like stems. Pruning these down in late fall leaves those open tubes exposed to the elements. Rain and melting snow funnel down the stems and collect at the base, causing crown rot and fungal decay in freeze-thaw cycles.

It has been revealed that it’s best to leave these old stems, faded flower spikes, and withered foliage in place to keep driving rain away from the vulnerable center. This dried top growth also traps air, forming an insulating buffer that protects the dormant buds huddled around the crown. So resist all heavy pruning until early spring, when fresh shoots begin pushing through the soil. Even if you live in a warm-winter area, it’s still best to leave major pruning until spring. The only fall cuts you should make are removing broken or diseased stems. Use sharp bypass pruners like the Felco 2 Bypass Pruning Shears, available from Amazon, when removing broken salvia stems.

It has been revealed that whenever I mulch plants for winter, I think of tucking a blanket around a sleeping child. Mulching salvias as cold weather is coming offers a layer of winter protection. When you apply mulch before the first hard freeze, you protect the root crown from severe cold and freeze-heave. In regions with fluctuating winter weather, bare soil expands and contracts, pushing shallow crowns up and exposing roots. Fully hardy salvia don’t need much winter protection, but a light mulch won’t hurt. When it comes to the semi-hardy salvias, however, mulching is a must to help overwintering plants.

In a recent development, the type of mulch, and how you apply it, are critical to avoid trapping moisture around the plant. Avoid dense, heavy materials like wet grass clippings, uncomposted manure, or thick leaf mold, which pack down and suffocate the plant. Instead, apply 3-4 inches (8-10cm) of loose, breathable mulch such as shredded pine bark, clean wheat straw, dry bracken, or horticultural grit. Keep it 2-3 inches (5-8cm) from the stems to avoid trapping moisture and inviting crown rot. Buy Bell Nursery Mini Straw Bales from The Home Depot for a loose yet insulating blanket.

Industry observers note that cold isn’t necessarily fatal for salvia plants in winter. But too much water will take out your salvias faster than a freeze. Native to sun-drenched Mediterranean climes, salvias demand sharp drainage. When sluggish drainage keeps soil saturated, oxygen is pushed out of the roots, leaving the crown vulnerable to fungal diseases. You’ll want to take steps to avoid poorly drained soil and winter wetness for any type of salvia.

It has been revealed that if your garden has heavy clay soil, take action now before winter sets in. Gently scrape away decomposing leaves, as wet leaf mats retain moisture over the crown. Work a handful of coarse horticultural grit, sand or perlite into the soil surface around the plant to speed up surface runoff. Back to the Roots Organic Perlite from Walmart is a great option for improving soil aeration and drainage around salvias. For container-grown plants, elevate the pots off cold, wet patio slabs. Use terracotta pot feet, pot toes, or bricks to ensure drainage holes remain clear of standing water.

If your salvia are tender varieties like Amistad or S. leucantha, treat them like the cold vulnerable plants that they are. Sub-tropical salvias can’t tolerate hard frosts or frozen soil. Leaving them unprotected in northern yards guarantees root death. Fortunately, tender salvias overwinter indoors with minimal fuss, provided you bring them into shelter before the first hard frost blackens foliage. If your tender salvias are in pots, trim the longest branches back by half, then move to an unheated garage, frost-free shed, cold frame, or cool porch, and keep at 35-45°F (2-7°C).

In a recent development, for tender salvias in beds, carefully dig up the root ball with a spade, keeping plenty of soil around the roots. Place into a plastic nursery container, backfill loosely with dry potting mix, and move it undercover. Use plant caddies such as the Bloem Plant Caddy from The Home Depot to wheel larger container-based salvias into the garage with zero strain or back pain. The goal is to keep the plant dormant. Water sparingly: just a cup or two a month keeps the root ball from drying out.

Even with meticulous winter care, an unseasonal polar vortex or prolonged freeze can challenge borderline-hardy salvias. Taking a few semi-ripe salvia cuttings provides a terrific insurance policy. Select healthy, non-flowering or semi-ripe shoots (or snip the flower tip off a vigorous stem). Take a 3-4-inch (8-10cm) cutting below a leaf node. Strip the leaves from the bottom half, leaving 2-3 pairs of small leaves at the top. Dip into a rooting hormone such as HydroDynamics Clonex Rooting Gel from Amazon, to seal cut stems and trigger root growth. Insert the cuttings into small pots filled with a 50/50 mix of sterile seed compost and perlite.

Water gently, then place a clear plastic dome or bag over the pot to maintain humidity. Set your baby cuttings on a bright, warm windowsill, but out of direct sunlight. They should root within 3-4 weeks. Keep them lightly watered through winter, and pinch the tips in late winter to encourage bushy growth. Just bear in mind that rooting will be slower now than it would be with cuttings taken in late summer or early fall. Grown on a sunny indoor windowsill or greenhouse bench through winter, your salvia babies will hopefully be ready to plant out next May.

It has been revealed that by the time spring arrives, you’ll be eager for warmer days and fresh growth (and so will your salvias!). As sunny afternoons begin warming the soil, check your overwintered salvias for vibrant green shoots emerging. That is your signal that winter danger has passed. You can then prune away old standing stems just above the fresh growth nodes. If you have woody salvias, spring is the time to shape the plant. Cut it back by a third to clean up the shrub. Spring is also the time to pull back protective mulches and reintroduce sheltered container plants to outdoor sunshine. With their crowns preserved through the cold months, your salvias will soon be rewarding you with months of lush and lively color.

  • In a recent development, for those with tweens and teens, this might seem obvious.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American kids are having a mental health crisis like no other. What are we to do with all these diagnoses?

Industry observers note that in a Upcoming York Time ideas story that ran this past week, Jia Lynn Yang opens with a bang: “One of the more bewildering aspects of the already high-stress endeavor of 21st-century American parenting is that at some point your child is likely to be identified with a psychiatric diagnosis of one kind or another. Many exist in a gray zone that previous generations of parents never encountered.”.

In a recent development, for those with tweens and teens, this might seem obvious. For those with younger ones, buckle up.

Recent findings suggest that in Yang’s story, she focuses on the role schools play. Failures in education may lead to an increase of psychiatric diagnoses like ADHD — alongside IEPs or maybe medications — as a means to catch up kids who are being lost in crowded, test-reliant, merit-funded schools. Of course, even Yang points out that schools are only one part of the puzzle. There’s screens and social media taking over our emotional lives and psychiatric development; the pandemic’s long-felt chilling effect on socialization; the adult world of division and anger in politics and everywhere else; and of course changes within the Mental Health Industrial Complex.

In a recent development, it’s this last piece that Dr. Sami Timimi, a child and adolescent psychiatrist and psychotherapist at the National Health Service in the United Kingdom is focused on. He's the author of six books including Naughty Boys: Anti-Social Behavior, ADHD, and the Role of Culture and his most recent book, Searching for Normal, which promises to outline a newly introduced approach to understanding mental health, distress and neurodiversity. There little doubt we could use some advice here — and a bit of demystification around the mental health crises that seems to have taken over childhood.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

In a recent development, I frankly found Searching for Normal to be a difficult book. The science and ideas are very clearly laid out, but you're throwing a lot of stones systemically and culturally that are not often cast. As a layperson and a parent with a house filled with diagnoses, medications, cultural shame, and lots of doubts about our mental health journey, the paralysis you describe feels very close to home. Given all this, I'm wondering, big picture, what is the main takeaway you'd want a parent to walk away with from your book?

It has been revealed that dr. Sami Timimi: It is a difficult read because we have a public narrative that's been around for a while that's really created a mythology around what we think of in terms of mental health and behavioral difference. My main message is that what we are calling psychiatric diagnosis aren't really diagnoses. And be careful where the culture of diagnoses might lead you to, because we have so much evidence now that the way we're approaching mental health has resulted in something called the treatment prevention paradox, where at a population level we're seeing increasing prevalence of mental conditions and mental health diagnoses. At the same time we're seeing an increasing number of people accessing various types of treatments associated with these diagnoses.

But we're not seeing an improvement in the outcomes. If we saw an improvement in the outcomes, we would expect at least a stabilization and hopefully a reduction in prevalence of certain conditions because they would be being effectively treated. I don't think there's actually much disagreement with this in most of the academic literature on what's going on because mental health does seem to be an outlier compared to we've seen a lot of progress in physical health.

For example, when I was a kid, if I got leukemia, my chances of survival into adulthood was around 20%. Now it's around 80%. So this is what happens when you have approaches that are built on technical knowledge that allows you to understand what's going on and make specific treatments for it. But it seems to be the case in mental health that we're going in the wrong direction. What are the assumptions that go missing when we approach mental health as if it's physical health? Because we have to remember, there's no brain scan for ADHD, there's no blood test for anxiety. You can't examine a thought under a microscope. And it becomes difficult to sit in that area of uncertainty and curiosity.

You talk about the TikTok contagion of health disorders and you cite the, I think it was 2023 research about Canadian teen girls presenting with a variety of self-described disorders that are all relatively rare. I'm wondering if you can describe the phenomenon and then I wonder, what does it change for parents on the ground? We have to take their thoughts seriously, no?

Recent findings suggest that yeah, that's a difficult one, isn't it? It's interesting because I heard about this research from a colleague and friend of mine who's a psychiatrist in Canada who shared this paper and it happened just at the point where I was seeing that in my clinical work as well, I was seeing young people who were brought by their parents, parents very worried, with presentations that are generally considered to be quite rare presentations. So, for example, I saw a number of kids who were coming and saying that they had these Tourette's symptoms but they had no history of it. It's like it suddenly emerged.

Sources indicate that it is hard because first of all, I don't blame social media for causing these things because actually a lot of this is narratives that's been suggested and started out. The bigger phenomena are these influencers who say that they have ADHD or autism or anxiety and they publicize it online and they talk about things that are signs of potentially having these conditions. And we have to remember, growing up is tough. Try to remember what I was like as a 13, 14-year-old — it is a struggle. There's a lot of changes going on.

You're in a phase of your life where you're seeking meaning and you're seeking belonging and you're involved in those existential type of scenarios where you're trying to figure out where do I fit in? What's my life all about? And so what's been happening is because they watch a lot of these things online with a lot of the influencers just taking up concepts that have been given to them by certain branches of academic psychiatry. And so what social media is doing is a kind of a social contagion. It's turbocharging these ideas and spreading them out.

This goes alongside a trend that's been happening in parenting.

Industry observers note that I think a lot of parents have lost their trust that they know what they're doing. I think a lot of parents have lost their confidence. They feel the need to go to see a professional to try and understand. And it's difficult when a lot of the professionals are also involved in what I call the Mental Health Industrial Complex. This is how they get paid, this is how they earn a living.

In a recent development, and so one of the things that I do encourage parents to do is don't be scared of your children. Don't be scared of their intense emotions and don't be scared of conflict. Conflict happens. What has I think happened as we've exported the knowledge base to professionals is we've also developed a curious form of something that some people refer to as cognitive parenting. I know the concept of helicopter parenting, cognitive parenting is a little bit different where you try to reason things through, where you treat your children as if they're already developed adults.

So what role should parents take?

If you don't think this is good for your children, tell them. If you want to put some boundaries around them, don't be afraid of their conflicts.

I liken it a little bit to a referee in, well, for us it's a soccer match. Whenever they, say, blow the whistle that there's a foul committed, the offending team that you've blown the whistle for will complain. That's what happens.

The crowd will complain as well and say the referee is biased and so on. So when you are a rule enforcer, one way to think about it is you're not going to get any good feedback. You're always going to get protests. You have to ride that out. But a good referee delivers the consequence. The consequence is usually fairly short, it's fairly immediate. Don't delay the consequences because you don't say, well, I've seen you doing that foul, but the next match you have, if you do that again, then the next match you have, I'm going to give this or that. Whatever consequence it is, immediate, short-lived, doesn't have to be long. Just something that reveals that you disapprove and this is not allowed.

And the other thing you do is you don't argue with them. So in soccer matches, you have a half-time where the teams go into the dressing room for 15 minutes before coming. You don't see a referee running after the player who's committed the foul telling them, “I've seen you, I've seen you doing this in other matches. You think you're going to get away with it. You never learn, you never listen.” A good referee spots the infringement, knows that they're going to get back chatted and they're going to get flak, needs to develop a thick skin to ride that out, not rise to it and doesn't get involved in nagging them and so on. And once the consequence is delivered, it's over. Don't need to talk about it again. It's finished.

What happens when you get caught in what you call the Mental Health Industrial Complex? A quote in the book that really resonated with me, asks “What might happen if instead of shaping the treatment around diagnosis, it was put to one side and the specific challenges, fears, and context were engaged with instead?” Can you answer the question you pose? What does that exactly look like?

So one of the things, understanding that what we call psychiatric diagnoses are not actually diagnoses, they're descriptions. They're what a branch of therapy referred to as narrative therapy ...[which] basically notes that our life is made up of stories. It's the stories we hear about ourselves, the stories others tell about us, and we build up a set of stories to understand ourselves. We're surrounded by narratives. And the narratives we tell ourselves have a powerful impact on how we experience our emotions.

Recent findings suggest that so what I was describing there is instead of falling down the root of imagining that if you get a diagnosis you found the meaning for what it is that is going on that's troubling you, there is a different way of trying to find out what it is you're trying to achieve, what is it the difference that you're trying to make, that a diagnosis can't do. So one thing I do in my clinical life is a form of what's referred to as Socratic questioning.

Industry observers note that let's say you got a diagnosis and it was the perfect diagnosis and you felt it fitted. What difference do you imagine this is going to make to your life? What difference is that going to make to your life?

According to recent reports, A diagnosis in a sense is an abstract thing. It doesn't really tell you specifically materially what's going on in your world. Is it that actually you're having trouble with friendships? Is it that your family is under stress and you're under stress because you think your parents are about to split up? Is it that you're finding yourself out of your depth at school? So you're trying to get to the specifics of what it is that people are wanting to see change in their life.

Sources indicate that right. Keep questioning the outcomes and ideas. I really like this tool for parents.

And the other thing is I'm trying to help people move past the idea that experiencing intense emotions is a sign that there's something wrong in them. Experiencing intense emotions is something that we all have to go through. If we don't go through it, we have less of a chance to develop psychologically.

Sources indicate that in a sense, the role of parents is to be careful about saving your children from struggle and suffering because that is an unrealistic goal. All life involves struggle and suffering at some level. How can we know joy if we don't know sadness? It's impossible.

Industry observers note that you say this is the most pathologized generation ever. Given that, do you have a checklist for parents to look through and say, is my child being pathologized?

Recent findings suggest that that's an interesting question. I may be averse to the whole concept of checklists, partly because in understanding that all our definitions of mental health are subjective. So our understanding of what is and isn't a kind of looming problem that needs some sort of professional intervention. There is no formula that will allow you to figure this one out. It's going to have to be situation, person and family specific.

Sources indicate that one thing I say to parents is, look, all good parents feel guilty. That's just a given. I cannot help you with that. Whatever I do, whatever anybody does, you'll carry on feeling guilty or worry, have I done too much of this? Have I interviewed too little? Have I given too much advice? Have I given the wrong? That's what good parents do. Be careful about that guilt driving you to do too much. And I think that's now a bigger danger than the opposite. So we end up intervening perhaps unnecessarily without holding our own anxiety and our own guilt. So one of my little messages is don't try too hard.

On that note, what do you do with the massive feelings in a household? How do you let challenges not get carried away?

Recent findings suggest that so one of the things that I try to work with with families is understanding, I use the metaphor of a dance, that there's emotional flow going between people and that emotional flow defines how that relationship works. And sometimes what happens is that anger becomes the dominant way in which connection happens.

It has been revealed that the other thing I think about in terms of emotions, I think of emotions as being viral. You catch the emotions of the person closest to you. If your kid is angry with you, it's very hard not to get angry back at them. So kind of developing an awareness of that emotional flow of how it's working in your particular relationship and developing an understanding that that has become a dance.

For example, I know there was a period in my own kid's life where there was a lot of tension, a lot of sibling rivalry to the point where our son and daughter were getting physical and losing temper. And we thought, me and my wife thought only one of them would survive in childhood. That's what it felt like to us.

Industry observers note that anyway, so I thought, okay, well I have to try and do something about this. So I started writing little post-its at the end of each day, just a few, a sentence or two about things that I liked that happened and I just stuck it above their bed before they went to bed.

After a couple of weeks of doing this, my daughter said to me, "Dad, you're being weird." And I said, "What do you mean I'm being weird?".

"Why do you keep putting these post-its and saying these nice things?" I said, "Okay, do you like it?".

So just something also a bit playful a bit, but it's just about trying to refine that emotional connection somewhere other than what's become the defining dance.

A little bit of, “all you need is love.” And I think you had it at the top of one of your chapters, quoting Confucius.

Sources indicate that exactly. The journey of a thousand miles starts with the first step.

#44494. Latest Update: It's Time to Stop Tracking Screen Time — And Start Living In the Digital Age

📅 02 Dec 2025 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3088 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: It's Time to Stop Tracking Screen Time — And Start Living In the Digital Age

📅 02 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, way too much falls on parents when it comes to screen time.
  • It has been revealed that the war for our kids' attention is being waged, and we’re losing.
  • According to recent reports, I’ve signed the Wait Until 8th pledge, I’m working on ways for the kids to be more independent (both commute to school themselves!), and we talk about screen time an annoying amount.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, way too much falls on parents when it comes to screen time. There’s another way.

It has been revealed that the war for our kids' attention is being waged, and we’re losing. That’s my cynical summary of so many experts who study such things. When it comes to screen science, I’ve attended the lectures, seen the documentaries, read the books, gone to parent meetups, and flipped through the studies. I’ve been through it personally with my high schooler — hooked, caught in dangerous situations, experiencing mental health crises thanks to the online world. My third-grader is phone-free and blissfully unaware (well, he loves Tears of the Kingdom, but that seems downright educational these days), but I still work so hard to get ahead of it.

According to recent reports, I’ve signed the Wait Until 8th pledge, I’m working on ways for the kids to be more independent (both commute to school themselves!), and we talk about screen time an annoying amount. Hell, I’ve helped to start and run a PTA committee whose purpose is to look critically at screen time and help foster independence in kids. There’s a lot of movement. And yet, it feels like parents are American revolutionaries in 1773. We’re dumping tea into the harbor and an impossibly well-funded army is coming to get us.

Industry observers note that this past week I took the fight overseas. I had the pleasure of talking with Kaitlyn Regehr, Ph.D., a researcher and professor of digital humanities at University College London and author of Smartphone Nation, out now. The tagline of the book is spot on: “Building Digital Boundaries When Offline Isn't an Option.” It’s a go-to book that’s informative, but not overly complex, exhaustive, but surprisingly short and to the point, and lacking in the shame that so many screen time books put on parents. I can't recommend it enough.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

In a recent development, I'd love to start with the idea of digital pyramids, if that's OK. Like the food pyramid, it can be a really helpful guide to how we and our kids should consume media. Would you mind just walking us through that idea?

It has been revealed that I think the idea of healthy eating is something we understand. The food pyramid, similar to the digital diet pyramid, is weighted with the good nutritious things at the bottom and the not-so-good things, the things that we want to limit, at the top. We might not always choose to follow it. We might sometimes eat a tub of ice cream, but we are aware that we are making that choice. I think what the digital diet pyramid does is it allows people and parents, most particularly, to think about the choices that they are constantly making every time they open a screen. Generally, what we want to do if we want a healthy relationship to screens is we want to be thinking about active, educational, informative, healthy socialization as forming the base of that pyramid. And then farther up the top are things like passive consumption, doom scrolling, short-form, low-quality content that we want to mitigate or moderate to a certain degree.

It has been revealed that in the digital pyramid, where do you place movies and cinematic video games? I think, these days, a kid who can watch a full movie or pay attention to hours of plot in one of those cinematic video games kind of has a leg up. Do you agree?

Sources indicate that right. So you are talking about long-form content versus short-form content and how that relates to the development of attention spans and the ability to follow full narratives through. Absolutely, not all screen time is created equal. What we want to be doing, where possible, is, of course, running around outside is normally better, but if you are going to use screens, we want that screen time to ideally be long-form engagement, like good quality movies, where possible, interactive engagement and collective viewing.

So particularly with young children, ideally, you are sitting there with them watching a Julie Andrews movie talking about the content, using it as a springboard for their discussion. If it takes place during World War II, maybe that is a discussion point for you to talk a little bit about history and use the viewing as a jumping-off point for education and for communication. That's where we really want to be with screen consumption, if we are going to be using those screens. Generally, the bigger the screen and the longer the content, the better.

So Mary Poppins over Roblox, that's my takeaway from this.

I appreciate how Smartphone Nation repeats the idea that screens aren't all bad and that the concept of “screen time” can shame parents for turning to screens ever. I think your book is a nice counterpoint to The Anxious Generation’s Jonathan Haidt, which primarily argues that taking away phones and getting kids outside is the answer. You note that being digitally native isn't all bad. So my question for you is, if screen time limits aren't the answer, where should we start?

Sources indicate that first, let's talk about where screen time comes from as a concept. Screen time, that guidance came out of some pretty good physical health research, mostly around childhood obesity and childhood diabetes from about 15 years ago. What that research said was, "If kids are sedentary, if they are sitting in front of screens all the time, they aren't moving around, that's bad for their physical health." That is still true. And Jonathan Haidt's argument around that is true. If you are in front of screens, you're not moving around, and that's not good for your physical health and aspects of your mental health, and I absolutely agree with that. But that guidance really just captured the quantity of the screen consumption, and not the quality of the screen consumption. So that guidance is limiting in that it doesn't address the mental health implications of what kids might be consuming on screens.

As we discussed previously, it's a very different scenario to have a kid watching with their parents Mary Poppins than for them to be alone in their bedroom with headphones on, scrolling through an algorithmically-driven feed. That is qualitatively a very different experience. The sad thing is that a Pew research study has recently pointed out that 89% of kids from the age of 5 are on YouTube now, an algorithmically driven, largely unregulated platform, and I think it's about 81% from the age of 3. Now, most of the discussions that we have at the moment around algorithms, around social media, completely leave out those younger years, and they tend to leave YouTube out of that discussion. But really for a lot of us, well-meaning parents, without realizing it, we're actually grooming our kids into these algorithmically-driven short-form, often low-quality content, from a really early age. So what we need to get to grips of is that not all screen time is equal and that we're actually needing to make an active choice.

Industry observers note that fortunately, there are many more choices available to us as parents than our parents had to make. That's not to say that we weren't plopped in front of screens to watch hours of content with bad-quality TV dinners (we were), but these were different screens and it was different content. Those were largely regulated spaces, often programmed by children's commissioners who were experts in programming children's content that had a diversity of content. You weren't watching 10 episodes of Bluey in a row. Those regulated spaces that a lot of good advocacy went into in order to develop, if we think of the development of children's programming on PBS, unfortunately, a lot of that good work has been thrown out the window because those kids are not on those spaces anymore, they're on YouTube, and that is a great tragedy.

Recent findings suggest that I think it's really important as parents that we remind ourselves that we are making choices. But because we are making choices, we can make different choices and we can make empowered decisions about the types of screens and the types of digital spaces we want our kids to inhabit. There's great empowerment in that I think.

In a recent development, you just mentioned how even Bluey could be problematic, which I've actually never thought about. It is a really good point. If you give the kid the control or you let it auto-rotate and do eight in a row, Bluey is a completely different experience. Whereas, usually, it's the safest possible space for parents with young kids.

I'm not saying that Bluey is problematic. It's not problematic. What is problematic is allowing a binge watching of an entire season. We actually should be having diversity of content. There are great things about curated spaces, and there are great things about children's programming that has carefully thought through what comes after what and that there's some kind of host that comes in and makes sense of things for kids. Terrestrial TV is a very different experience. When I speak to my kids who are still very little about healthy screen consumption, I talk about terrestrial TV. I talk about algorithms and the fact that algorithms make our choices for us. It's vital that we're active in our decision-making and that there are experts and, in the post-truth world, it's worth acknowledging, that there are some people that curate viewing experiences and these are regulated spaces. That means that that's a different experience so that there are healthy forms of screen consumption and less healthy forms of screen consumption.

Industry observers note that now, that is not to say that running around outside is still a much better thing to do. Of course, it is. But if you are going to use a screen, it's good to be much more intentional about how you do it.

In a recent development, if I can move to a slightly older audience. I have a teen myself, so I think about this all the time. How do I stop my kid from getting red-pilled?

When we talk about online extremism or the echo chambers that our kids or our uncles or ourselves might be in, I think it's really crucial to take a step back and think about the technological processes at play. The reason that young boys are often fed online misogyny or more extreme content is because it is more attention-grabbing. The reason that girls are fed body dysmorphic content and self-harm is because it's more attention-grabbing. The financial structures of social media are an attention economy. The whole system is set up to hold our attention as long as possible and, in fact, hold our attention a little longer each time. Unfortunately, that often means that hate, harm, and disinformation are often algorithmically prioritized because they are more attention-grabbing, because disinformation is often more attention-grabbing than truth.

One of the best things we can do, and we absolutely should be doing this with teenagers, is talking about that concept, talking about the attention economy, talking about the way in which we are manipulated through social media, and our usage and our behaviors online are collected in order to manipulate us, just to hold us a little bit longer. If you talk to kids about this idea, even from early teenage years, they don't like it. They don't like the idea of being emotionally manipulated and controlled. One thing that I talk about with any type of echo chamber is instead of fighting or debating your teenager or uncle at Thanksgiving dinner around the specificity of the glitch, around the granular detail. It's better to take a step back, collectivize, and talk about the ways in which these technological and corporate structures are feeding them this content and pushing them potentially down a narrower and narrower path.

And then it becomes you together against those structures, and that becomes a very powerful thing. One, you are equipping your young person with tools to be empowered digital citizens, and, two, it's something you're in together because you yourself are not immune to it and you are probably being fed something different, but it may be something that makes you feel bad.

Industry observers note that this one's for parents of neurodivergent kids. It seems that we are getting pulled in two directions. On one hand, social media is more dangerous. One study you cited mentioned that the likelihood of seeing self-harm content is, tell me if I'm getting this right, 40% greater for those with mental health difficulties, 31% greater for kids with autism. On the other hand, you also write that evidence suggests that screens can provide predictability and a sense of belonging within like-minded communities and can be instrumental in helping neurodiverse kids manage anxiety. Can you please walk us through this?

It has been revealed that I think this goes back to this idea of quality consumption and the choices that we make around our screens. That work around social media-fed harm or algorithmically-prioritized harm and the way in which neurodiverse kids are disproportionately targeted is immensely problematic, and, if you have a neurodiverse child, something you should be aware of. That is not unique to neurodiverse children. Social media is very, very good at predicting our behaviors, but also at knowing our vulnerabilities because it is through those vulnerabilities that it can point out [what we] lack and we are more susceptible to buying things if we feel a lack. That fits into this business model. The work that has been done around the way in which screens can support neurodiversity tends to be around ways in which screens can be used to calm kids, ways in which different learning applications can support neurodiverse kids, and that there are ways in which differently abled kids might find community through the internet. That remains true and those are good things, but of course we're almost talking about different usages of screens. That stuff is not happening on TikTok in the same way. It just really isn't.

Recent findings suggest that A lot of the discussions that we used to have around the beauty of social media a decade ago and the way it gave platforms for speaking voice and finding community has shifted as the technology has become more and more sophisticated and more and more manipulative. When we talk about that good stuff, we really need to be careful about how we're carving out those spaces, what screens we're using to do them, and where those screens are being used.

In another sense, keep kids away from the algorithms.

In a recent development, yeah. For younger teenagers, I tend to find that algorithmically driven content is more and more problematic. As these systems become more and more sophisticated, they will be able to hold our kids' eyeballs longer and longer and longer, and we have to push back against that.

It's hard to do forever, of course, even if we hold off social media until they are 16. That birthday will come, and they will turn 17. What we want to be doing is preparing our kids. Just like you would teach them how to drive, you would prepare them and you would talk to them about the dangers and you would talk about how to use it safely.

Recent findings suggest that hear, hear. You acknowledge throughout this book that so much falls on parents that shouldn't, that the dark recesses of this online culture we're fighting is not our fault, but it is the fault of corporate profits and lack of regulation. What do you say to us burned-out and angry parents? I wonder, you seem so pragmatic, are you angry at all at this world?

Yes, absolutely. I am like an angry mama bear, but I do think that there is power in that anger too and I think a movement is starting. I am hopeful, because if there is enough of us that are angry, we will see change because policy follows the public will. But I do acknowledge that, at the moment, so much is heaped on individual responsibility in a way we don't have for anything else. We're used to consumer protections. We're used to consumer protections around the food we eat, the medication we take, the cars we drive, the small parts on kids' toys so they don't choke. We are used to being protected, and we're not being protected in this space and our kids are not being protected in this space. There is a newness in that. Most things have to be proven safe before they hit the market. For social media, the opposite has been true.

Sources indicate that now, unfortunately, that means that the duty of care and the responsibility is right now falling on us as parents. So while we wait for regulation, while we wait for greater corporate responsibility, we need to know that if our kids are going to inhabit this space, they're doing so without seat belts, and that's why we need to educate ourselves as parents. We need to do that work. I think that doesn't make it our fault. This is not our fault, but we do need to learn these things or else our kids will be forced to navigate it alone.

In a recent development, on the flip side, how do we fight? How should we join the movement? What's your advice for those of us who want the anger to spill out in the public space?

In a recent development, this is why this book is not written in the way that other books are, which is often from a mental health perspective. That's not my expertise. I operate in the digital space. I'm talking about how these technological processes work so that you yourself can be informed about them and you can push back against it. I think if enough people understand that, if enough people read this book, they will say, "This is crazy. This is totally crazy that we've allowed this to happen," and that's when you will see policy change because, ultimately, that's how democracy works. If you think of really successful grassroots movements, it is because people inform themselves and they think it's no longer acceptable.

Gary Vaynerchuk Just Wants Us All To Be (And Raise) Nice Guys

📅 13 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2202 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “I have all of my validation, and I mean all of it, wrapped up in being a nice guy.”.
  • In a recent development, if you haven’t seen Louis Theroux: Inside the Manosphere, make a date with Netflix.
  • Recent findings suggest that in the documentary, Theroux, the understated British journalism, calmly and a bit coldly explores the manosphere from the inside.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I have all of my validation, and I mean all of it, wrapped up in being a nice guy.”.

In a recent development, if you haven’t seen Louis Theroux: Inside the Manosphere, make a date with Netflix. This is must-see TV for parents, especially parents raising boys. But a word of warning, it’s like a scary movie that will haunt you well after the credits run. Weapons has nothing on the horror show that is the manosphere.

Recent findings suggest that in the documentary, Theroux, the understated British journalism, calmly and a bit coldly explores the manosphere from the inside. In talking to the most extreme influencers — the peddlers in misogyny and anti-semitism, conspiracy and homophobia — he finds himself pulled in to the fight, made into content, taken out of context, and expertly trolled, even as he holds the camera. “He really don’t wanna be in the live,” one such British influencer says to the camera in front of Theroux on a particularly disturbing night out. “He don’t wanna be on the content. But he’s got no choice.”.

Recent findings suggest that we parents, on the other hand, do have a choice — to shield our kids from the depravity, to push back against the cultural creep, and to turn to other influencers. Influencers like Gary Vaynerchuk, the best-selling author, radio host, entrepreneur, and an unabashed dude who plays his part as the antidote to the vitriol of the manosphere. As an executive — CEO of VaynerMedia and Chairman of VaynerX — he’s a hard-nosed, fast-talking entrepreneur who believes in bootstrapping life. He also fundamentally believes in kindness. “I know I was well parented,” he tells Fatherly, “and I have all of my validation, and I mean all of it, wrapped up in being a nice guy.”.

Parents can choose to be nice, sure, but Vaynerchuk also notes we can choose to be more accountable, to stop coddling our kids on one hand while taking charge on the other (taking away their social media access or phones if we need to). “Supporting your child is everything,” says Vaynerchuk. “Enabling your child is a disaster.” And walking that tightrope between the two? That’s parenting.

The following interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

Recent findings suggest that gary Vaynerchuk is an unapologetically wealthy entrepreneur. But his empasis on self-improvement and kindness poses an important question: What’s the point of being rich if you’re an unhappy jerk?

What do you think is the real reason people are checking out — from the workforce but also social life — and how can we inoculate our kids, and especially boys, against this?

Recent findings suggest that gary Vaynerchuk: I think modern parenting has lost its way. I think we've made a couple of crucial mistakes, and we're blaming it on social media because we don't like accountability. Mistake number one: I do think, especially for boys, we got a little too into eighth-placed trophies, a little too "fighting isn't the way to resolve things", a little too coddle-y-coddle-y. Listen, I'm a mama's boy through and through. I also got into ten fights in school, and my mom had no opinions about it, meaning it was like, "Yeah, life." I think we've gotten too in our kids' business. Again, everyone grows up in different circumstances. There's plenty of kids right now that don't have parents in their business.

It has been revealed that forget about the '80s and '90s. From the '70s and '60s, '50s and '40s, '30s and '10s, '00s, and on back to the 1800s … parents did not go to school and yell at teachers for giving their kid a B instead of an A. But that is what has happened the last 20 years. ... The f*ck are we texting our sons who are 27 because we have the family f*cking proposal and knowing where everyone is? Let men be men.

Who do you think wins in a fight: a lion that grew up in the Bronx Zoo, or a lion in the jungle?

We've raised a lot of zoo lions in the last 25 years. We need to take a little bit of our foot off the pedal.

What role do you think sports play in teaching some of this wildness, some of this conflict?

In a recent development, I think it's everything. When my son was growing up, during a game, if there was a kid that cried when they lost, I used to, with the parents' permission, I would be like, "It's good that you're crying kid. Don't listen to your parents." Multiple parents were happy that I was doing that for their kid.

Industry observers note that I think if you have a kid that cries when they lose in sports, you've been given a blessing. And I think you should compound that, not suppress it. Teaching your kids that nothing matters is a bad idea — leads to depression. If someone said to me around a game of monopoly tonight, "Bro, it's just a game." I'd be like, "F*ck you, man. This is life. When I play, I'm playing for life." So I think sports is everything, but I think parents get involved too much yelling at the coach. Let the coach cook — even if the coach sucks.

Let [your kid] deal with a sucky coach, because you're going to have a sucky boss. Dad's going to have a sucky day. You're going to have a sucky governor one day in your life. Get used to people that have authority or leverage over you. You're going to interact with a sucky policeman. You're going to have a sucky doctor. You have f*cking 27-year-old men throwing temper tantrums because they never were taught how to deal with sucky authority.

Industry observers note that talk to me about humility. How do we get more of it?

In a recent development, sports is where I learned humility, and it is my superpower. My mom would've not raised a humble child. I thought I was Superman. I literally thought I was the most athletic and most handsome person on earth somewhere around fourth grade. Because in my neighborhood, I had the best hand-eye coordination. And in my neighborhood, I was a little bit better athletically … I won a lot, and then it started to change. And that was a rude awakening. I mean, going through the journey of humility, first getting used to the taste.

According to recent reports, I would lose, play again. I would lose, play again. I annoyed people. I feel it's now coming clear to me, literally in real time right now with you, I feel like in second, third, fourth grade, I might've had excuses. So it took some time to acquire that taste, but much like caviar, much like sweetbreads and truffles … oysters, that initial [taste] is like, "Oh, it's a little weird.".

Recent findings suggest that and now I love the acquired taste. [Similarly] I now love humility. I love it. It got me here. And now that I'm, quote-unquote, "at some level of success", and I know people look at me, I love that the kids see my humility in meetings behind the scenes. I hope it inspires them to realize it's a beautiful trait, not a loser trait.

In a recent development, you recognize losing is learning. There's a sweetness to that.

Brother, I'm a little bit even weirder. I like losing. I swear to God, I like it, man. I like adversity. I like it. I'm addicted to the underdog, when someone's an underdog, and then they become the champ. Or the reverse; Kobe, Tiger Woods. Tiger, early, loved, loved [them] early. But then I was like, when he was the main guy, I was like, "Ah.".

I’d like to jump into something you've said before and my wife and I use it a lot: "Your kid is not your friend." I have a teen right now. I think that truth has kind of hit me hard fairly recently. Do you still believe that, and why? What's the motivation behind it? What's the evidence?

It has been revealed that I mean, the evidence is I'm 50 fucking years old and I get 10,000 DMs a day, and I read the content, and I analyze the content. If you're not the person for your child that teaches consequences and ramifications, it's going to be a problem. They'll learn it. Life will teach them, starting at 22, which ... F*ck, man, to unlearn 22 years of that behavior ...

Industry observers note that listen, supporting your child is everything. Enabling your child is a disaster, and that is a fine f*cking line. It's been amazing in so many ways to watch the generation of women that are [now] 48-years-old and are straight best friends with their 15-year-old daughter. Kids are older, and parents are younger, so it makes sense to me. I think it's actually beautiful, but I think there's a lot of moms who lose the plot in the beauty of ... the nirvana of such a gorgeous relationship, and I think they feel the ramifications later, and they need to be eyes wide open.

It has been revealed that being friendly is amazing. You know [parents tell me], "No, Gary, you don't get it. I want them to come to me. I couldn't go to my mom." Yeah, your mom was treating you inappropriately too far in the other direction, but they come to you because you're their f*cking drug dealer. You're dealing the drug of non-accountability. You're dealing the drug of no consequences. You're giving them a little hit of, "It's everyone else's fault but yours.".

I'm wondering how that practically plays out when it comes to money. How do you teach your kids about money, the hustle, the passion, work?

According to recent reports, very easy. You stop giving it to them. And the question becomes, when? I have a major thing of 15, 16, 17, 18 feels in the right range. My parents make fun of me on this. If they watch this, they'll call me and be like, "Eh, eight, nine, seven, 10." They were earlier. But, man, I will say, and this is tough, because I know a lot of dads are going to hear this, if you have a 23-year-old son who you're giving money to, you are destroying that child. They have to stand on their own two feet financially. Look, the old days, AKA the '80s and '90s, kids did borrow money from parents to get their first home, but they paid them back … with interest. That's a foreign concept.

Industry observers note that let me just drop the atomic bomb on everyone that I unearthed eight years ago. Let me get you all to the punchline: If you have a 27-year-old right now that you're giving money to, he's saying all the right things to you in your face, but let me tell you what he's thinking at 11:00 at night when he takes his second Tito's on the rocks: he thinks that you think he's a loser.

I don't know if you not paying for your kid is going to make them financially successful. I do know it's going to make them a man. I just did another podcast earlier. I'm doing a bunch today. Someone said, "Who do you admire?" I said, "Somebody that works two jobs and takes care of their family, and doesn't complain.".

#44489. “Do I Have To Go To College?”
