    #44421. As A Therapist, I Thought Caregiver Burnout Wouldn’t Come For Me. I Was Wrong.

    📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1101 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

    As A Therapist, I Thought Caregiver Burnout Wouldn’t Come For Me. I Was Wrong.

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1101 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The sandwich generation is sorely lacking in support.
    • Recent findings suggest that tuesday, 8:10 p.m.
    • In a recent development, after months of juggling my work as a therapist with caring for my aging mother (who has been diagnosed with dementia), and being a present, engaged mom and wife, I had to admit that I was dropping some balls.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The sandwich generation is sorely lacking in support.

    Recent findings suggest that tuesday, 8:10 p.m. I’m helping my 87-year-old mother brush her teeth and change for bed. My 10-year-old calls from the room next door that he and his dad are done reading his latest Significant Nate book. He asks (again) when I’m coming to his room to say goodnight. I try not to rush my mother, but I’m exhausted after a long day, and keenly aware of missing those precious minutes right before bedtime when you get the real deal from your child about everything that happened that day.

    In a recent development, after months of juggling my work as a therapist with caring for my aging mother (who has been diagnosed with dementia), and being a present, engaged mom and wife, I had to admit that I was dropping some balls. Having all of this on my plate was clearly not working.

    Recent findings suggest that I knew I was not alone — I’ve been having this conversation with many friends and clients, also in their 40s or early 50s. In fact, 47% of caregivers under the age of 50 are part of the sandwich generation, those of us who are raising children and caring for aging parents at the same time. If we aren't talking about perimenopause with all its patches and pills, we’re talking about the health concerns of our parents and, potentially, our grandparents as well.

    The burnout I was feeling falls particularly heavily on the shoulders of women. Even if you have siblings, most of the caregiving responsibility consistently falls on one person, and that person is typically a woman. Women shoulder the majority of caregiving responsibilities, often to the detriment of their careers. To make matters worse, some caregivers may have a complicated relationship with the parent who is now dependent on them.

    Industry observers note that caring for your parent can be immensely rewarding and depressing. Sometimes I feel deeply honored to care for the person who dedicated her life to caring for me. Other times, my mom can’t remember why her beloved husband hasn’t come home yet — my father passed away several years ago. She really doesn’t enjoy having to be bathed by her child, for that matter.

    As a mental health professional who has sat with clients going through this very thing, I expected to have more of the answers, to be able to cope and balance more than someone else due to my experience. But the truth is, nothing can truly prepare you for your induction into the sandwich generation.

    No matter how we try to overcome the difficulty of caregiving as individuals, we must acknowledge that there’s minimal financial or systemic help for consistent care for the elderly living at home. Some Medicare programs can provide all your healthcare in one place, which is obviously better than driving all over town talking to doctors who aren’t talking to each other. But they often only offer last-minute daily help and, because of the high need in our country, you typically see a fresh caregiver each day. While better than nothing, it’s clearly not a great situation for a parent who is already confused in their day-to-day life. Some programs actually pay you, the caregiver, for your work, but that doesn’t give you back the missed moments with your own children or restore those career opportunities.

    Recent findings suggest that eventually my husband and I realized that we needed help. Fortunately, we could afford to pay a nurse out of pocket, but the costs have been steep: tens of thousands of dollars annually to have carers for my mother seven days a week, and that’s with me still doing bedtime duty on the weekends. It’s simply not realistic or sustainable for most people.

    And one of the challenges that we don’t often talk about is the guilt. Even if you are able to defy the odds and pay someone to come in to help, you still feel guilty about it and get caught up in the “shoulds.” I should be able to care for my parents and my children at the same time; people have been doing this forever with a lot less help. I should be grateful to be able to spend whatever time I have left with my parent. The notable part missing from that is the fact that many of us don’t have villages in the way we used to — that nearby family network that would support each other during all the stages of life.

    Our lack of a village came into focus for me recently when we adopted a baby into our family. She has brought us more joy than we could have imagined, and I see how much a community would change this experience for us. In my Mommy and Me classes, so many of the young mothers have discussed having their parents come and stay with them during the early weeks of having a newborn. What a stark contrast for me as a mother, in a different phase in my life, where I am taking care of my parent, rather than her taking care of me and my children.

    This is a problem that is not going anywhere. Around the country and the world, people are making tough decisions every day — draining bank accounts, missing out on kids’ milestones, declining promotions and date nights with their partner — to take care of a loved one. The physical, financial, and emotional toll can cause extensive damage to the caregiver’s well-being in so many ways.

    Recent findings suggest that we also know what to do about this problem. Studies show that while caregiver burnout is a worldwide glitch, it is less so in the countries where (surprise, surprise) there is a strong public healthcare system, flexible work environments for caregivers, and affordable private health insurance. These kinds of safeguards can be a key part of rebuilding a upcoming kind of village and community support. The answer is there. The question is if we will take heed before we all burn out.

    Sources indicate that dr. Patrice Le Goy is a licensed marriage and family therapist and international psychologist. She is also the research chair of Maternal Mental Health Now and the board chair of Open Paths Counseling Center, as well as the host of Like-Minded with Dr. Patrice, an award-winning mental health podcast.

    Patrice lives in Los Angeles with her husband, two children, and their massive dog who is definitely part wolf. You can follow her on social media @drpatricelegoy.

    #44420. My Parents Took Me Voting. Now I'm Doing The Same With My Daughter.

    📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1421 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

    My Parents Took Me Voting. Now I'm Doing The Same With My Daughter.

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1421 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that your candidate might not always win.
    • It has been revealed that my earliest memories of voting take place at the elementary school up the street from my parents’ house.
    • At the time, I didn’t think of any of this as civic education.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that your candidate might not always win. But, as my parents taught me, it’s notable to show up anyway.

    It has been revealed that my earliest memories of voting take place at the elementary school up the street from my parents’ house. Every Election Day, my parents would bring me and my younger sister along with them to the polls. I remember standing in the long lines impatiently wondering when it’d be our turn. I remember at least one year where there was a mock ballot for kids. And, perhaps most importantly to elementary-school-aged me, I remember receiving the prized Future Voter sticker at the end.

    At the time, I didn’t think of any of this as civic education. My parents weren’t necessarily sitting us down for lectures about democracy or giving us pop quizzes on the Voting Rights Act of 1965 (although that would come later during my AP U.S. Government class). My parents were simply voting and we were watching. But, as it turns out, we were learning by observing.

    Sources indicate that my parents made it abundantly clear to my sister and me that voting was both a right and a responsibility — and that this wasn’t always the case for people who looked like us. As Black girls growing up in America, that history mattered. We learned that Black people had marched, organized, been beaten and even killed for the right my parents exercised so routinely at the elementary school around the corner.

    In a recent development, so, when Election Day came around, we went. And not just for the presidential elections every four years. My parents participated in every election — local, federal, didn’t matter. The responsibility was the same.

    By the time I was finally old enough to vote myself, I couldn’t wait.

    I missed being able to vote in the 2004 presidential election by a year, which meant the 2008 election would be my first chance to vote for president. And I felt elated that my first presidential vote would be for the country’s first Black president.

    According to recent reports, at the time, I was working as a reporter at my community newspaper in a conservative county in Maryland. On Election Day, a colleague and I spent hours driving around to various polling places, interviewing voters and reporting on turnout before returning to the Board of Elections to wait for results.

    After work, I went home and watched the national returns with my dad. When Barack Obama walked onto the stage in Chicago’s Grant Park with his beautiful Black family, I remember staring at the television in disbelief.

    According to recent reports, wow, I thought to myself, soaking in the moment. I just witnessed history.

    But elections don’t always end with the history you hoped to witness.

    In a recent development, in 2016, I proudly cast my ballot for Hillary Clinton and went to bed believing we were about the elect the country’s first woman president. We all know how that turned out.

    Recent findings suggest that four years later, I voted for Joe Biden, but I was especially excited about his running mate, Kamala Harris, whom I’d supported in the Democratic primary. Watching a Black and Asian woman become vice president meant something different to me. Of course, representation isn’t the only reason to vote for someone and I think we’re all doing ourselves a disservice if we pretend as if identity is entirely separate from politics. As a Black woman in America, I’d spent most of my life looking at the highest echelons of power and rarely seeing anyone who looks like you.

    Recent findings suggest that in the spring of 2024, I picked up my then two-year-old daughter Violet from daycare, went to swim lessons and then swung by our neighborhood elementary school to vote in the Illinois presidential primary. With her little puffs and binky in tow, she naturally became the star of the polling place.

    Our next-door neighbor, Mr. Steve, was working the polls that day and gave Violet a Future Voter sticker. She was entranced. To her, the sticker was probably the best part of the whole outing, which, when I thought about it, was exactly how I felt when I was her age (and, let’s be real, is also how I feel as an adult).

    Afterward, we went outside to the school playground and, as I watched her run around, it hit me what a full-circle moment this had become. And then I had another thought: This could be a children’s book.

    I wanted to write a book that could explain voting to children around Violet’s age: something that would talk about walking into a polling place; why grown-ups stood in line to fill out ballots; what even is a ballot; and why any of this matters anyway.

    That fateful afternoon eventually became the premise of Violet Goes Voting, an early reader about a little girl accompanying her parents to the polls and learning that voting is one way we use our voices. But the book was just the beginning.

    That fall, my husband and I took Violet with us when we voted in the presidential election. This time, I had a very specific picture in my head of what the moment might look like in both real life and the book version. My daughter would sit on my lap as I cast my ballot to elect the first Black woman president of the United States.

    It has been revealed that my parents had taken their Black daughters to the polls so we would understand that our voices mattered. Decades later, I would take mine with me as I helped elect a Black woman to the White House. Except, of course, that’s not what happened.

    Like so many people, I woke up the next morning devastated. The history I had imagined sharing with my daughter would have to wait. Since then, I’ve thought a lot about what, exactly, I want Violet to inherit from me and learn from all of this.

    Industry observers note that because maybe the lesson was never supposed to be that if you show up, your candidate will win. My parents certainly never promised that to me. What they taught me was the importance of showing up anyway.

    Voting is a small part of civic engagement, but it was my introduction to it nonetheless. Long before I knew what a primary was, before I understood the harsh reality of voter suppression or could name any of my congressional representatives, before I was old enough to fill in a bubble next to a candidate’s name, I knew what Election Day looked like.

    Recent findings suggest that it looked like my parents making time to go to the polls. It looked like my sister and me eagerly tagging along. It looked like waiting our turn. And, yes, it looked like getting a sticker at the end.

    Industry observers note that now, as a mom, I understand that those seemingly ordinary trips were teaching me something much bigger: This is what our family does. We show up. We pay attention. We responsibly exercise the rights people before us fought to secure. We don’t take them for granted.

    Only time will tell who Violet will vote for when she’s old enough to cast her first ballot. And, frankly, we have a while before that happens. She’s much more interested in playgrounds than politics at the moment, which is exactly how it should be for an innocent five-year-old.

    But I hope that when her first Election Day arrives, she’ll look back on our family selfie from outside the voting place in 2024. I hope she’ll remember me reading to her the book that she inspired. I hope she understands why walking into that booth and making her own choice carries a history older than the both of us combined.

    Industry observers note that but most of all and most importantly, I simply hope she reveals up. Because that’s the inheritance my parents gave me and my sister. And now it’s mine to pass on.

    L’Oreal Thompson Payton is an author, journalist and the founder of Zora’s Place, a Black feminist bookstore and community hub in Evanston, Illinois. Her books include Stop Waiting for Perfect, Amanda Gorman: Poet and Activist, Violet Goes Voting and the highly-anticipated memoir Infertile Black Girl (Fall 2027). Her byline has appeared in outlets such as Essence, Fortune, Newly introduced York magazine and SELF. Learn more at lorealthompsonpayton.com.

    #44419. How to Stop Birdseed Getting Wet in Feeders This Fall – and Why it's Vital You Bother

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1158 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    How to Stop Birdseed Getting Wet in Feeders This Fall – and Why it's Vital You Bother

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1158 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A rainy week in fall can turn a full feeder into a clump of wet, sour seed that's unsafe for birds to eat and a waste of your hard-earned money.
    • Industry observers note that A backyard feeder can still look full from the kitchen window after a couple of rainy days in a row, but get closer and you'll see the seed inside has darkened and packed into a wet plug above the ports.
    • So, knowing when it's safe to dry bird seed, and how to keep it from getting soaked in the first place, is an essential part of feeding birds through fall and winter.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A rainy week in fall can turn a full feeder into a clump of wet, sour seed that's unsafe for birds to eat and a waste of your hard-earned money. A few simple changes to your bird feeding set-up to keep seed dry, however, keeps both your feathered friends and your bank balance a lot happier.

    Industry observers note that A backyard feeder can still look full from the kitchen window after a couple of rainy days in a row, but get closer and you'll see the seed inside has darkened and packed into a wet plug above the ports. In some cases, you can dry out the seed, but soggy birdseed costs more than the price of the bag. Damp seed quickly grows mold and fungi, some that release harmful toxins that can cause fatal infections in these beneficial garden friends. Wet grain also gives harmful bacteria an easy start and parasites a place to survive, turning a crowded feeder into a disease hotspot. Some seed decays into a mush that small birds can't safely digest, too.

    So, knowing when it's safe to dry bird seed, and how to keep it from getting soaked in the first place, is an essential part of feeding birds through fall and winter.

    Sources indicate that good seed isn't cheap and you'll find plenty of bird-feeding advice online recommending spreading wet grains on a tray to dry out. That suggestion comes with a catch, however. If the birdseed got damp in a recent rainfall just after you filled the feeder an hour ago, then go ahead and dry it out so you can feed it to your garden birds. However, seed that's been sitting soaked inside a feeder or has been out in all weathers for days is likely contaminated, and there's no good evidence that drying makes contaminated seed safe again.

    You see, if a bag of birdseed just got wet on the garage floor an hour ago, a gust blew rain across the scoop on the way to the feeder, or the bag sat open by the door during a drizzle, you know that seed is likely still clean. But seed in a feeder is a different story: birds have been perching on it and leaving droppings, harmful bacteria may be multiplying in the damp conditions, or parasites and pathogens may be present. So, the safer call is always to throw soggy birdseed out.

    In a recent development, if you're confident the birdseed is clean and only recently wetted, spread it on a clean baking tray or fine mesh screen, one seed deep if you can, and leave it to dry indoors in a warm room where the air moves. A rimmed baker's pan like this from Walmart keeps seed from rolling off. Stir the seed occasionally and, once it pours loosely again, it's safe to feed. If the seed smells at all musty or indicates any fuzz while it's drying, though, toss it out.

    It's an easy call to throw out birdseed if it's moldy, clumped together, smells musty or sour, or looks darker or discolored compared to when it went into the feeder. But even if the seed still looks normal, it may still carry mold or bacteria which can affect bird health – fungi can grow inside a seed's shell and often there's nothing on the outside to give it away. So, if you ever find yourself wondering is wet birdseed safe, bag it up for the trash and keep your backyard birds safe.

    Industry observers note that bird experts recommend cleaning a bird feeder every 1-2 weeks in winter, and it's wise to clean it whenever it gets soaked through, too. It's a good idea to give your feeders a quick look after any heavy rain: if the seed doesn't shift freely when you tip the feeder to one side, it needs cleaning. The more often you clean a feeder, the quicker and easier the job becomes, especially if you use diluted white vinegar to clean bird feeders, so it needn't be a chore.

    According to recent reports, empty out the wet seed, take the feeder apart and scrub each piece in hot, soapy water. It's easier with a long brush with straight and curved ends like this Songbird Essentials 2-in-1 feeder cleaning brush from Walmart. Clear each drainage hole with a toothpick, too. Rinse thoroughly then let every piece dry completely before refilling and hanging up the feeder. Rake up any wet seed and hulls under the feeder as well.

    Sources indicate that of course, the best solution to one of the most common bird-feeding problems is to prevent the seed getting wet in the first place. Many hanging feeders come with a dome or rain guard that sits above the seed tube to keep the worst of the rain off the ports, but they're rarely big enough to provide effective protection. Adding a more robust layer of protection, like this bird feeder rain guard from Amazon that comes in either a 16-inch or 19-inch diameter design with a snap hook to clip the feeder on underneath, is far more effective and doubles as a squirrel baffle, too. For a hopper feeder, look for a design with a roof that overhangs the ports and has drainage holes in the base or, on a tray feeder, a mesh bottom that lets rainwater run straight through.

    Sources indicate that keep feeders away from roof edges and gutters where runoff pours straight down, and during wet spells, only put out as much seed as birds will finish quickly. Keep birdseed dry in storage, too, by using a lidded container that mice can't chew into like Behrens Galvanized Steel Can from Home Depot.

    In a recent development, making sure you don't leave soggy birdseed in feeders is an vital part of helping backyard birds survive winter. Just like taking steps to stop your bird bath freezing over, this is an easy job for us gardeners that's hugely beneficial for our feathered friends. There are so many ways to feed birds through fall and winter, from planting a berry-bearing shrub to feed birds through winter to saving kitchen scraps and using the lard-smear trick that makes sure smaller songbirds get their fair share of food, and it's a joy to help our garden visitors. But if you're choosing to offer a nutritious supply of grains, do make sure you're not serving up any fatal fungal spores alongside by keeping birdseed dry.

    Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

    #44418. 22 dietitian-approved lunchbox snacks you can buy off the shelf

    📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (892 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mother ↗ Open Full Page

    22 dietitian-approved lunchbox snacks you can buy off the shelf

    📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Packing a lunchbox snack shouldn’t require a degree, but the snack aisle makes a decent case otherwise.
    • According to recent reports, labels promise real fruit, no artificial anything and a good source of something.
    • Recent findings suggest that robin Barrie Kaiden, MS, RD, CDN, CSSD and Lauren Manaker, MS, RDN, LD, both do the same thing with a newly introduced product before it goes in the cart: They turn it over and read.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Packing a lunchbox snack shouldn’t require a degree, but the snack aisle makes a decent case otherwise.

    According to recent reports, labels promise real fruit, no artificial anything and a good source of something. The truth is, most of it is noise. The part that matters is on the nutrition label. For a run of dietitian-approved lunchbox snacks you can buy and pack as-is, we asked two registered dietitians who shop that aisle for a living what they actually look for.

    Recent findings suggest that robin Barrie Kaiden, MS, RD, CDN, CSSD and Lauren Manaker, MS, RDN, LD, both do the same thing with a newly introduced product before it goes in the cart: They turn it over and read. Here’s what they’re looking for, and the snacks they reach for without overthinking it.

    Sources indicate that kaiden scans the label’s ingredients first. “That matters to me more than anything else,” she notes. She wants simple, real-food ingredients and the least processed option available. There’s a practical reason to start there, notes Manaker. Ingredients appear in order by weight, so the first few make up most of the product.

    Recent findings suggest that the claims on the front get much less of their attention. “Made with real fruit” doesn’t tell you how much fruit is actually in there, claims Kaiden, and “no artificial flavors” doesn’t automatically make something a nourishing snack. Even the regulated claims are narrower than they sound, explains Manaker. “Good source of fiber” means the product provides 10 to 19% of the daily value per serving. “Gluten free” matters for kids with celiac disease or a gluten sensitivity and does nothing nutritionally for anyone else.

    The label lists added sugars and total sugars separately. Total sugars include the naturally occurring sugars in ingredients like fruit and milk, says Manaker. Added sugars are the ones put in during processing, and those are the numbers to take into consideration. The targets for added sugar are lower than most parents expect. The Dietary Guidelines for Americans recommend no added sugars for children under 10, and the American Academy of Pediatrics advises less than 25 grams, about 6 teaspoons, per day for kids 2 and older.

    Kaiden also looks at where the sugar comes from. She passes on high-fructose corn syrup and would rather see a small amount of honey, maple syrup or coconut sugar. “Those are still added sugars, so the amount matters, but the source and processing matter to me, too,” she says. If cane sugar is on the list, she prefers it farther down.

    Protein and fiber make a massive difference in how satisfying a snack is. Kaiden balances a carbohydrate-rich food with protein and some healthy fat, like fruit with nuts, cheese or plain yogurt. “That combination helps slow digestion and supports steadier energy through the afternoon,” she says. For a substantial afternoon snack, she suggests around 5 to 10 grams of protein and at least 3 grams of fiber, depending on a child’s age, appetite and activity level. Those numbers can come from the snack as a whole. No single bar has to do everything.

    Most U.S. children don’t get the recommended amount of fiber, notes Manaker, so small additions help. Fruit, veggies, beans, whole-grain bread or crackers, and nuts or seeds where school rules allow are all easy lunchbox sources.

    Hydrogenated and partially hydrogenated oils are an automatic no for Kaiden. Partially hydrogenated oils contain industrial trans fats, which are particularly harmful to heart health. High-fructose corn syrup, a highly processed sweetener that adds sugar without meaningful nutrition, is another pass.

    Sources indicate that seed oils get a lot of negative press, but Kaiden’s position helps clear up confusion: When there’s a comparable option, she opts for extra virgin olive oil or avocado oil instead of seed oils because of the difference in processing. Many seed oils are extensively refined, and some are extracted using solvents such as hexane. “That processing is why I personally prefer other options,” she says, “not because all seed oils are harmful or because using hexane means unsafe amounts remain in the food.”.

    She’s also not rigid about it. Some Simple Mills crackers contain sunflower oil, and she still buys them for the almond-flour base. “I look at the whole product rather than letting one ingredient make the decision for me,” she indicates.

    Unfamiliar names aren’t automatically a problem, either. Ascorbic acid is vitamin C. Tocopherols are forms of vitamin E that can help preserve freshness. “I care more about what an ingredient actually is than whether its name is easy to pronounce,” indicates Kaiden.

    Read the ingredients even on brands you buy regularly, Kaiden cautions, because formulations change, and one good product doesn’t mean everything from that brand makes the cut.

    To make shopping easier for you, we asked the nutritionists exactly what they’re tossing in their carts. Take notes!

    Industry observers note that kaiden’s favorite snack doesn’t sound like a dietitian’s pick at all. “Potato chips!” she states, naming José Andrés Extra Virgin Olive Oil Potato Chips, made with potatoes, extra virgin olive oil and salt. “I want my kids to enjoy their food, and a simple-ingredient chip can absolutely fit into a balanced lunchbox. Add a sandwich and some fruit or vegetables, and you have a lunch that’s nourishing and enjoyable.” Potato chips? Say less.

    The Busy Mom’s Guide To Gift Shopping On Budget

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Amazon and Alexa for Shopping make it easy to get it all for less.
    • Amazon knows how hard moms are working, and they have some ways to lighten the load.
    • With everyday low prices that meet or beat other retailers across a huge selection of products, from affordable private-brands that help you save without sacrificing quality to the name-brand finds your kids have been asking for, Amazon makes it easier to find gifts that fit your budget.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Amazon and Alexa for Shopping make it easy to get it all for less.

    Amazon knows how hard moms are working, and they have some ways to lighten the load. When you shop through Alexa for Shopping — Amazon’s personalized agentic shopping assistant — it all becomes way less stressful and way more affordable, and you might even get enough time back to finish your coffee before it gets cold (can you imagine?).

    With everyday low prices that meet or beat other retailers across a huge selection of products, from affordable private-brands that help you save without sacrificing quality to the name-brand finds your kids have been asking for, Amazon makes it easier to find gifts that fit your budget.

    Here are a few ways to use Amazon to get all the gifts you need — and stay sane while doing it.

    Alexa for Shopping is Amazon’s agentic shopping assistant, and it’s really something else. It combines knowledge of the hundreds of millions of products across Amazon with info from across the web, and applies all of that to your personal shopping history and preferences. In other words, it knows all the possible gifts you could get on Amazon, and it knows you.

    Industry observers note that you can use Alexa for Shopping by asking it questions, like “What are the best toys for 5 year-olds?” or “What are teenagers asking for this year?” or even “What are some premium and more affordable brand options for a red dress and matching headband for my 3 year-old daughter’s holiday outfit?” It will give you ideas (including taking your shopping history and preferences into account) and then share a list of products to look through. So whether you’re gifting your own kids and just need some fresh ideas when you’re drawing a blank, or shopping for an older niece who lives five states away and have no clue where to start, you get tailored advice that helps you land on the perfect thing.

    It has been revealed that budgeting during the holidays is not for the weak. Between finding the perfect gifts for your kids, your mother-in-law, and your spouse, it’s easy to get caught up in the excitement of holiday shopping and discover more things you know they’ll (or you’ll) love along the way.

    It has been revealed that the good news? Amazon’s prices consistently meet or beat other retailers, so you’re already getting low, competitive prices when you shop on Amazon. On top of that, Alexa for Shopping is a great tool to help you stay on track. First of all, you can use it so see up to a full year of price history for any product you’re interested in. Once you have that information, you can ask Alexa for Shopping to let you know when it drops to the right price for you. And even better, you can ask Alexa for Shopping to turn on auto-buy so it can complete your purchase using your default payment method when the item reaches your price target.

    That saves you time (who has the bandwidth to keep checking back every day?!) and helps you know that when you do hit “buy” (or have Alexa do it for you), you’re getting the thing you want at a great price. And if you do that for all of your holiday shopping, you’re setting yourself up to spend less this season. That can be a huge relief at such an expensive time of year.

    Bonus: the savings aren't just about gifts. From stocking up on groceries for the holiday feast to getting extra household essentials for overnight guests, the season comes with plenty of demands. With everyday low prices on fresh groceries and household essentials, plus fast free delivery, you can get the things you need at great prices that help your holiday budget go further.

    A large part of the mental mom load is figuring out which [insert kid-related item here] is the best one. From onesies to bikes to pimple patches, there are so many things to choose from, and it takes time to figure out what’s actually right for your kid.

    Recent findings suggest that alexa for Shopping takes that stress off your plate, too. Once you’ve found a few options that might work, Alexa for Shopping’s got you: it can show you side-by-side comparisons, highlighting the differences in features, price points, and even the reviews. Instead of digging through details, you get it all laid out and can swiftly make your pick. Goodbye, overthinking.

    It has been revealed that we all know that holiday magic is really just... moms. But Amazon and the features built into Alexa for Shopping sort of feel like their own kind of magic. With Amazon, you can create a holiday season your kids will always remember, and make it look almost effortless. When you can do that without overspending or screaming into the void? We think that’s beautiful.

    (And heads up, the savings go even further with Prime thanks to free delivery, exclusive deals, gas discounts, and more. But we digress.).

    The best kind of holiday magic isn't just finding the right gifts at the right prices. It's getting a little time back for yourself, too. And honestly, moms deserve that kind of magic most of all.

    #44416. Buy These 6 Perennials “Bare-Root” This Fall – You'll Save Money and Enjoy Gorgeous Flowers for Years

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1210 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    Buy These 6 Perennials “Bare-Root” This Fall – You'll Save Money and Enjoy Gorgeous Flowers for Years

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1210 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, when shopping for upcoming perennials, you’ll often find the choice of potted or bare-root plants.
    • But bare-root planting isn't all about saving money.
    • Industry observers note that while there are many reasons to add bare-root plants to your garden in fall or spring, it's best to give them four to six weeks to establish roots before the ground freezes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, when shopping for upcoming perennials, you’ll often find the choice of potted or bare-root plants. Bare-roots are dug up while dormant and shipped without soil around their roots. Since they’re lighter, they’re easier and less expensive to ship – which is why many plants sold online arrive bare-root.

    But bare-root planting isn't all about saving money. Planting during dormancy lets plants focus more energy on developing strong, healthy roots. Cooler temperatures and often rainier conditions are ideal for many bare-root plants, minimizing stress during the transfer.

    Industry observers note that while there are many reasons to add bare-root plants to your garden in fall or spring, it's best to give them four to six weeks to establish roots before the ground freezes. This is later than your first frost date, as the soil usually takes longer to freeze. Check when the ground is likely to freeze in your area before choosing and buying bare-root perennials.

    According to recent reports, if you're out of time for the season, late winter or early spring is another great time to do this. However, it's worth ordering your plants in fall, as many nurseries sell out of popular varieties well before spring. You can often order now for delivery at the right planting time.

    It has been revealed that when your perennials arrive, their roots should be wrapped in moist material. Keep them wrapped until you’re ready to plant to prevent the roots from drying out or becoming stressed. First, choose the right location based on the plant’s soil, moisture, and sunlight needs. Then, prepare the soil by pulling weeds, loosening it, and adding compost.

    Industry observers note that once you’re ready to plant, unwrap the roots and inspect them. The roots should be firm and plump. Trim off any mushy, brittle, or moldy roots, but avoid cutting into healthy roots. If the roots aren’t very moist, soak them in water for 30 to 60 minutes before planting.

    Industry observers note that plant the roots in a hole large enough to fit them and let them spread out, following the recommended planting depth for each plant. Before planting, sprinkle a mycorrhizal fungi inoculant, such as Xtreme Gardening Mykos Mycorrhizae from Amazon, directly over the roots and in the planting hole. These beneficial fungi form partnerships with the roots of many perennials, helping them absorb water and nutrients.

    Industry observers note that backfill the hole with soil, gently firming it around the roots to remove any large air pockets. Give the plant a thorough watering to help settle the soil, and continue watering as needed to keep it moist until the ground freezes. Finally, apply a light layer of mulch around the plant to help retain moisture and protect the roots from temperature fluctuations over winter.

    Peonies bloom with large, beautiful flowers in late spring or early summer, and they are among the longest-lived of all garden perennials. This makes bare-root peonies an excellent investment. Plant peonies in an area with fertile soil, excellent drainage, and full sun.

    Fall is a good time for bare-root peonies. Plant them so the eyes, the small growth buds, sit 1 to 2 inches (2.5 to 5.0 cm) below the soil surface. Planting them too deeply will prevent flowering.

    Eden Brothers currently has a sale on peony roots, and my pick is this beautiful Pastel Mix Collection. Or try the Jumbo Mix for the most flamboyant flowers.

    Another popular flowering perennial, daylilies are adaptable, forgiving, and easy to grow. They flower in summer, with each bloom lasting only a day, but with an ongoing parade of new flowers for weeks.

    Eden Brothers' Fragrant Rebloomer Mix is a great place to start, or for containers, the Stella de Oro Daylilies from Burpee are small but impactful.

    Plant daylilies in full sun or partial shade in well-drained soil. They generally do well when planted as bare roots in fall, but allow them a few weeks to establish before the ground freezes over. Otherwise, wait until spring. Plant the crown no deeper than one inch (2.5 cm) below the soil.

    In a recent development, this classic perennial blooms in late spring and early summer with some of the garden's most striking flowers. Their frilled petals on top of tall stalks come in many colors – I adore these pastel coral-pink Beverly Sills Irises from Burpee, as well as these pale blue Sea Double irises.

    In a recent development, bare-root bearded irises come as root rhizomes that you can plant four to six weeks before the first hard freeze. Plant them in full sun and soil that drains very well. If you live in a region with cold winters, timing is essential. If it’s too late now, wait until spring. When planting, lay the rhizomes horizontally in the soil, with the upper surface just barely covered.

    Like irises, oriental poppies offer frilled, colorful, and striking flowers on stately stems. They add drama and structure to beds with late-spring and early-summer blooms in shades of bright orange and red, and even pink and white. They grow best in full sun and well-drained soil.

    As long as they have time to establish, you can successfully plant bare-root poppies in fall, though these stunning Harlem Oriental Poppy Roots from Jackson & Perkins will ship in the spring. Take care when choosing a location for poppies. They develop long taproots that don’t transplant well.

    Industry observers note that astilbe plants are known for their plumes of feathery flowers that bloom in shades of red, purple, pink, and white in summer. Astilbe thrives in partial shade, or even more shade, and rich, moist soil. Younique Pink Astilbe from Burpee is a lovely compact variety for containers, while Mighty Chocolate Cherry Astilbe from Jackson & Perkins reaches over 6 feet, making it a striking border option.

    Recent findings suggest that you can plant bare-root astilbes in fall if they have enough time to establish, or in the spring. Plant to a depth that keeps the crown at soil level.

    This is another shade-friendly perennial suited to woodland gardens and beds with partial or full shade. Bleeding heart blooms in spring with characteristic heart-shaped flowers that hang from gracefully arching stems. Choose a spot with moist but well-drained soil.

    Bleeding hearts don’t tolerate being moved very well, so choose your spot carefully. Get them in the ground in fall with plenty of time to establish. The crown should be one to two inches below the soil surface with the eyes facing up.

    Eden Brothers sells Bleeding Heart Roots Mix to preorder for spring, or pick up a bleeding heart bare-root from Spring Hill Nurseries at Walmart for fall planting.

    Industry observers note that bare-root perennials are a good investment if you take the time to plant them right. They cost less than potted plants and can give you years of reliable blooms with good care. If you’ve missed the fall window for planting these in your region, make your selections over the winter and order them for a spring planting, another excellent time for most bare-root plants.

    Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

    #44415. Industry News: "Covert Contracts" Might Be Wrecking Your Relationship

    📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1648 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: "Covert Contracts" Might Be Wrecking Your Relationship

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1648 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you’ve ever thought “after everything I do,” therapists say you might have one.
    • In a recent development, you did bedtime solo every single night this week.
    • According to recent reports, so when Saturday morning rolls around, you’re planning to sleep in.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you’ve ever thought “after everything I do,” therapists say you might have one.

    In a recent development, you did bedtime solo every single night this week. You did the baths, with all the splishing and the splashing and the bubble anarchy. You fielded the lightning round of existential questions at 8:47 p.m. (“Mommy, what happens to doggies when they die?”). You tucked everyone in and then did your regular closing-time routine to get the rest of the house buttoned up for bed.

    According to recent reports, so when Saturday morning rolls around, you’re planning to sleep in. You fully expect your partner to wake up and handle the kids, the breakfast, the early morning dog walking duties. The whole shebang. Tit for tat.

    Industry observers note that then your kids are in your face before you can even pry your eyes open, wondering where their soccer cleats are or if you can get more juice. Cue the rage, right? OK, so here comes the uncomfortable gut-check… did you communicate your expectations to your partner? Or did you just sort of assume it was a done deal?

    This scenario has been dubbed a "covert contract," and therapists say it can lead to a whole lot of resentment building up in a relationship over time. Here’s what experts want you to know about where this behavior comes from, how to spot it in your own actions, and how it differs from the imbalance of the invisible load.

    “A covert contract is a deal only one person signed,” says Kristyn Carmichael, Esq., a family mediator, certified divorce financial analyst, and founder of Couples Solutions Center. “It sounds like ‘If I do X, you’ll do Y,’ but the other partner never saw the terms, never agreed to them, and usually doesn’t know the contract exists.”.

    Industry observers note that and she often has a front-row seat to what happens when those deals go unaddressed for a prolonged period of time. “In mediation, I see the end stage of these: one spouse arrives with years of unpaid ‘invoices,’ and the other is honestly confused about what they owe.”.

    According to recent reports, cheryl Groskopf, an anxiety, trauma, and attachment therapist who authored The Somatic Healing Workbook, likens it to writing a massive ol' agreement and assigning your partner an equally big role in it. Somehow, your partner is the only person unaware of stated agreement.

    But your partner being unaware doesn’t change the way you feel. The hurt is just as real as if they’d actually broken a promise. “In your brain, they did,” Groskopf explains.

    Sources indicate that um, yes. One hundred percent. This was something every expert agreed on! However, the need itself isn’t the issue here; it’s the delivery method.

    “The need underneath is reasonable, but if it’s not articulated overtly, then it’s unreasonable to think your partner would be a mind reader,” says Dr. Jenni Skyler, Adam & Eve’s resident sex and relationship therapist.

    Industry observers note that already, as a busy working mom who happens to be the default parent, I instinctively start to feel myself bristle at this idea. No one tells me these things or what needs to be done — I just notice and do it because someone has to. The experts say that sort of thinking is a fast path to frustration.

    “‘I want my partner to make an effort on my birthday’ is a totally reasonable desire,” Groskopf notes. “‘I shouldn’t have to tell them what I want because if they really loved me, they’d already know’ is when it becomes problematic.”.

    Now, the experts were also abundantly clear that none of this means moms should just silently accept an unfair split.

    “One person also shouldn’t have to become a household manager simply because they are more organized, quicker to notice what needs to be done, or less comfortable leaving things unfinished,” says Ilona Phillips, a psychotherapist and founder of Lotus Consulting in Ann Arbor, Michigan. “Expecting shared responsibility is reasonable. Expecting a partner to recognize an unspoken sacrifice and reciprocate exactly one-for-one can get partners in trouble.”.

    Sure there is: Asking is scary.

    “If I ask for a break and you say no, that’s a direct rejection,” Carmichael says. “If I never ask, I’m protected from that, and I keep the moral high ground.” And, yes, there’s also that belief so many of us carry that “if I have to ask, it doesn’t count,” she adds, “as if a gesture only proves love when it’s unprompted.”.

    That belief tends to run deep, too (ask me how I know). Says Groskopf, “If you grew up learning that your needs were inconvenient, asking can feel incredibly vulnerable.” Instead of just asking, we end up creating these little litmus tests our partners don’t even know they’re taking.

    She uses flowers as an example. If you ask for them, you know they indicated up because you asked. But if your partner brings them on their own, "There’s this feeling that you were appreciated, that they noticed you, that you MATTER. And for someone who grew up feeling overlooked or emotionally neglected, that distinction can feel huge.”.

    Oof. The catch here is that this strategy often just backfires.

    Sources indicate that “There is a fear that if we directly communicate what we need, and that need is not met, we will be hurt,” explains Dr. Paulette Didia, a licensed clinical psychologist in Fresh York City. “However, if we do not communicate what we need, our partner will not know, our partner will not do it, and we will be hurt anyway. We think hurting in our own mind ‘hurts less,’ and that is not true.”.

    Industry observers note that admittedly, the lines are a bit blurry. When you’re doing the lion’s share of invisible work in your home and family, it’s hard not to “keep score” or have a running tally in your head of what your partner did versus what you did.

    Unfortunately, that scoreboard warps how both partners see each other.

    “Once you develop a narrative that your partner isn’t doing enough, it becomes very easy to fill that bucket with examples of how they’re falling short. Meanwhile, your spouse feels like they’re always in the doghouse and starts to wonder if it’s even worth trying. One person is thinking, ‘Don’t you see how hard I’m working?’ while the other is thinking, ‘What did I do wrong now?’” says Mary McLaughlin, LCSW, a couples therapist and discernment counselor.

    Recent findings suggest that so while it’s fair to feel frustrated by an invisible (or visible) load imbalance, a little communication can go a long way. That’s true on both sides of the line. “Even if the score is unequal, if all parties know the score and acknowledge it and offer gratitude, this can offset resentment,” says Skyler.

    In a recent development, well, obviously this is tricky since you probably don’t know you’re making them. However, there are a few tells you can look for, according to the experts:.

    First and foremost, resist the urge to try settling years of “back pay.” You can’t Uno Reverse this one. Instead, focus on rewriting the terms and making sure you and your partner are, in fact, on the same page. Here are a few practical pointers from our pros on how to pull that off.

    Make the invisible more visible.

    According to recent reports, didia asks couples to fill out a simple weekly worksheet together that includes tasks along with who does them and when. She has couples do this at the same time each week so that it doesn’t become one more thing Mom has to track, and they post the list where both can see it so no one becomes the default reminder.

    If you want to follow suit, start by listing every task (significant and small). Next, let each partner choose what they’ll take, and split the ones nobody wants. Very vital info: The person who owns a task decides how and when it gets done. “Maybe you think this should be done by Monday, but your partner indicates it will be done by Wednesday,” Didia notes. “Since it is their task, they get to decide and, by Tuesday, you will not already be annoyed.”.

    Gauge your relationship’s temperature.

    Recent findings suggest that phillips encourages a weekly check-in where partners take turns asking: What’s been working well between us? Is anything feeling off? Extra difficult? Frustrating as hell? Unacknowledged? And, finally, how can I be a better partner to you this week?

    Don’t swap one test for another.

    Sources indicate that you may be tempted to stop doing certain things, like washing the dishes, hoping that someone will notice. That’s just a covert contract in a different outfit, states Phillips. And even if your partner does pick up the task, resentment can still linger. You might then think, Why did I have to stop before they noticed?

    Sources indicate that “Relationships change. What worked when you were first dating, before kids, 10 years ago may not work anymore,” reminds McLaughlin. “Couples need to renegotiate instead of assuming the old arrangement still works.”.

    In a recent development, when you realize you’re locked in a pattern that won’t budge, it’s probably time to see a couples therapist. Carmichael’s advice is to get help sooner rather than later. By the time couples land in her office, she notes the covert contracts show up even in how they divorce, i.e., “I gave up my career, so I deserve more.”.

    At the end of the day, adds McLaughlin, “Resentment paired with avoidance is a particularly risky combination for couples.” And that means the fix, both annoyingly simple and incredibly hard, is saying what you need out loud… and holding each other accountable to those needs in a way that feels fair and equitable to you both.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that each November, Google gives us a peek behind the curtain, synthesising billions of shopping-related searches into their Holiday 100 Gift Guide. The list is built from a full year of Search trends across every category from tech to style. And this year, the toys and games section looks suspiciously like the inside of an elder millennial’s childhood toy chest.

    Here are the trending toys parents will want to know about, plus what the list says about how we’re shopping this year.

    According to recent reports, searches for “classic toy train set” climbed 240% this year, one of the biggest jumps Google shared. Wooden trains survive toddler teeth, being thrown down the stairs and never fail to get passed down more than once. (Expect the figure-eight to claim your living room floor for the next few years.).

    “A ton of play,” Google wrote, and we respect the pun. Searches for stuffed elephant plushies rose 240%, with the Pets Alive Baby Elephant Surprise as the featured pick. Plush is a good pick for a 1-year-old and a 10-year-old alike, and the right one becomes a friend for life.

    In a recent development, searches for the Fujifilm instax holiday set jumped 190%. For tweens, a camera that spits out a real photo is a nice break from the phone, and the prints end up taped to bedroom walls instead of buried in a camera roll. They’ll fly through the film, so tuck a couple of extra packs in the box.

    Searches for the FAO Schwarz Piano Mat “struck a chord,” rising 180% in 2026. Anyone who watched Tom Hanks stomp out a duet on the giant keyboard in “Big” wanted one of these, and the floor-sized version now fits in a playroom. It’s a sneaky music-and-movement toy for preschoolers. It’s also loud, so choose its permanent residence carefully.

    Searches for “adjustable roller skates” cruised up 180%. Adjustable skates expand across several sizes, so they can outlast a growth spurt or two. Just remember to add a helmet and pads to the cart.

    Some of this may come down to who’s doing the shopping. Millennials make up a big share of today’s parents, and plenty of us spent our childhoods at the roller rink, building wooden train tracks across the living room rug and waiting for Polaroids to develop. (By impatiently wagging them back and forth, of course.) It’s not hard to imagine a few of these searches coming from parents trying to hand down something that felt magic to them. The best part? There’s a good chance they’ll all still be in rotation when next year’s list comes out.

    Breaking: 10 Foreign True Crime Documentaries To Scratch Two Itches At Once

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Travel the world or curl up on the couch to watch true crime documentaries?
    • Travel the world or curl up on the couch to watch true crime documentaries?
    • It has been revealed that how do you scratch both of those itches?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Travel the world or curl up on the couch to watch true crime documentaries? Why not do both?

    Travel the world or curl up on the couch to watch true crime documentaries? It’s the universal conundrum. On the one hand, the world is a major and beautiful place full of opportunities to eat delicious food and meet latest people and wear hats you would never wear at home. On the other hand, there are true crime stories that need to be solved by you in your pajamas on the couch under a weighted blanket.

    It has been revealed that how do you scratch both of those itches? Well, you could travel the world seeking out true crimes to solve yourself, but that would get pricey and probably pretty dangerous. You don’t want to become the subject of your own true crime documentary, after all. Instead, settle in on a long, rainy weekend (or when it’s bright and sunny, I’m not judging) to watch these engrossing true crime documentaries set in beautiful locations around the world. It’s safer and the snacks are cheaper.

    It has been revealed that in 1996, French film producer Sophie Toscan du Plantier was found murdered outside her remote holiday cottage in the small village of Toormore. West Cork two days before Christmas. Sophie was just 39 years old and mom to son Pierre-Louis. A local journalist was one of the first to report her murder, and promptly became the main suspect. Netflix’s three-part docuseries Sophie - A Murder in West Cork covers not only Sophie’s tragic death, but also the struggle between Ireland and France to convict the killer.

    Amy Lynn Bradley was just 23 years old when she went missing from the Royal Caribbean cruise ship Rhapsody of the Sea one early morning in March 1998. The ship was en route to the island of Curaçao. Her room revealed no sign of a struggle, and several items were left behind. Authorities initially considered Bradley’s disappearance to be a potential accident or suicide, but Netflix’s 2025 three-part docuseries Amy Bradley is Missing speculates on several other possibilities that could have happened in the sunny tropics.

    It has been revealed that we do not love a scam artist. Especially one who preys on women looking for love, as Israeli conman Shimon Hayut aka Simon Leviev did between 2017 to 2019. Hayut swindled millions of dollars from women in the Netherlands, Norway, and other countries around Europe, leaving them destitute and broken-hearted. That’s the bad news. The good news is the way these women eventually found each other, banding together to bring Hayut to justice and try to reclaim their money. Netflix’s 2022 documentary The Tinder Swindler tells the story of three women who lost nearly everything to Hayut, and how they came together to bring him down.

    Sources indicate that the Netflix 2026 three-part docuseries Should I Marry a Murderer? will stay with you for a long time after the fact. Not just because it’s set in the gorgeous Scottish countryside, but because of the perspective it offers on what it might actually look like to find out the man you love is genuinely a murderer. Caroline Muirhead met handsome Scottish farmer Alexander “Sandy” McKellar on Tinder, and the two got engaged in 2020 after a whirlwind four month romance. When McKellar confessed to a murder that happened three years earlier, Muirhead stays with him. Told from her modern day perspective, Should I Marry a Murderer? Is an unflinching glimpse at what we might be willing to overlook in the name of love.

    Vittorio Emanuele was nine years old when his family was exiled from Italy in 1946. His father was King Umberto II, and Vittorio was meant to be a prince until Italy voted to create a republic without the royal family. Living a life of luxurious exile, Vittorio was on the French island of Corsica in 1978 when he was involved in the death of 19-year-old German tourist Dirk Hamer. Netflix’s 2023 three-part series The King Who Never Was features interviews with Vittorio himself, as well as Dirk Hamer’s family members who were determined to see the privileged deposed royal charged with Dirk’s murder.

    Monique Olivier: Accessory to Evil.

    It has been revealed that michel Fourniret confessed to killing 11 women and one man in the picturesque Ardennes region of France between 1987 to 2003, making him one of the most notorious serial killers in modern French history. The Belgian killer only confessed after his seemingly submissive wife, Monique Olivier, provided police with enough information to force his hand. Which meant, of course, that she knew something of her husband’s crimes. More than police might have suspected, if the 2023 Netflix limited series Monique Olivier: Accessory to Evil proves anything. Olivier might have even been a willing participant in her husband’s horrific crimes. Chilling.

    Fair warning for the 2019 five-part Netflix docuseries Who Killed Little Gregory? - the entire series revolves around the awful kidnapping and murder of 4-year-old Grégory Villemin in a small village in eastern France. Grégory’s murder has never been solved, and this docuseries delves into the disturbing allegations that members of his own extended family might have murdered the little boy. This one is equal parts difficult to watch and completely engrossing.

    If you’re looking for some real-life Scandinavian noir to get you through the dark nights of fall, you’ll want to check out The Lørenskog Disappearance, Netflix’s five-part docuseries based on the true story of real life Norwegian billionaire Tom Hagan. Hagan’s wife Anne-Elisabeth Hagan went missing from the couple’s opulent home in October 2018, and a ransom note asking for nine million euros was left in her wake. The police originally believed Anne-Elisabeth was kidnapped, but began to suspect murder when the alleged kidnappers didn’t continue to reach out. While this 2022 limited series is a drama and not a straight documentary, it really delivers on Scandi vibes and billionaire intrigue.

    The Lie: The Murder of Grace Millane.

    In a recent development, british tourist Grace Millane was taking a gap year to travel the world when she ended up in New Zealand in 2018. She planned to head back home to her family for Christmas. She never made it back home. Millane was reported missing by her family, with police conducting a massive search in Auckland and the surrounding area before zeroing in on Jesse Kempson, her final Tinder date. The 2024 documentary The Lie: The Murder of Grace Millane on Amazon Prime, features interview tapes with Kempson as he is interrogated by police, and his subsequent attempt to use the so-called “rough sex murder” defense for killing the 22-year-old. On her birthday.

    If you’ve been thinking of spending a bit of time in the UK along the coast, the Apple TV series Coastal Killers will either intrigue you or scare you off, depending on your perspective. Instead of focusing on just one true crime story, Coastal Killers has eight seasons of stories of mayhem in lovely little seaside towns in the UK...

    ...Which should keep you busy as you proposal your next potential trip.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Charlotte York – ahem, I mean Kristin Davis of Sex and the City fame – recently demonstrated off a Thanksgiving centerpiece that would look perfect on any table this fall.

    Much like Catherine Zeta-Jones, Kristin has taken a DIY approach to her Thanksgiving decor, using homegrown pumpkins in a very different way to the usual tried-and-tested Halloween methods.

    It has been revealed that in the clip (which you can watch here), Kristin can be seen tucking a glass jar of sunflowers into a gutted pumpkin, transforming it into a vase. And, if you're interested in copying the look, I've consulted a few experts to help.

    Shop A Cheat Version Of Kristin Davis's Pumpkin Vase:.

    If you want to steal Kristin Davis's Thanksgiving decor for yourself, the trick is to treat the pumpkin as a container, not a planter.

    “Choose a firm, unblemished pumpkin, cut the top wide enough to fit a glass jar, and scoop the inside completely clean, because leftover pulp shortens the life of both the pumpkin and the flowers,” says Morgan Brooks, founder and editor of Plant Style Home.

    Nadi Melam, founder of Florals Memories, insists that you should “choose a pumpkin that’s flat with a large opening (slightly wider than it is tall, this will mean it’s lighter!)”.

    Industry observers note that the experts at Almondsbury Garden Centre insist that the jar element of Kristin Davis's Thanksgiving decor is non-negotiable. “Once hollowed out, place a glass jar or small watertight container inside to hold the water,” they say.

    “This is crucial as pouring water directly into the pumpkin can cause it to soften and rot more rapidly.” Brooks adds a practical bonus, saying “it lets you change the water every two days without disturbing the arrangement, which matters more for freshness than any floral preservative”.

    Melam says most leaks and wilting come down to the same few things, all of which can be staved by the jar. “Dry off the pumpkin, choose a tight-fitting jar, remove all the leaves below the water line, and you will solve most of your problems.”.

    When it comes to filling your pumpkin vase, Melam has a tip for choosing your flowers, saying, “The most beautiful flower in the shop is the one with the least amount of time left in its life.” Look for buds that are just opening, because “when the bud first begins to open, there is still its prime to come.”.

    At home, Brooks claims to “Cut the stems at a sharp angle, strip every leaf that would sit below the waterline, and condition them in warm water for an hour before arranging.”.

    According to recent reports, your next step is to build around your arrangement. “Sunflowers carry heavy heads on thick stems, so place them first as the structure of the arrangement and fill around them with smaller fall flowers and foliage,” states Brooks.

    Recent findings suggest that reilly Renwick, designer and creative lead of State of the Wall, indicates the secret to recreating Kristin Davis's Thanksgiving decor is a tight palette. He says, “The key is to keep it thematic. Not just fall-themed, but dialed into a specific palette of colors that complement each other instead of standing out individually without coherence.” He does have one warning: “Fall colors are, to no fault of their own, awfully close to compost colors.”.

    In a recent development, because sunflowers are so large, he suggests pairing them with “smaller blossoms, like alstroemeria, gypsophila, or small roses.” And don’t let the arrangement block the view across the table. “If in doubt, just keep it at 12 inches or shorter,” claims Renwick.

    The pumpkin fades first, so Melam advises making it ahead of time: “I’d suggest you put this together a day or two in advance and keep it in a cool place until needed.”.

    Recent findings suggest that to keep costs down, raid your own garden. “If you have zinnias in your garden, your problems are solved,” claims Renwick, who also recommends dahlias, marigolds, asters, and mums. Almondsbury suggests, “Using flowers and foliage from your own garden, such as autumn asters, dahlias and ornamental grasses, and adding just a couple of sunflowers for impact.”.

    When Thanksgiving is over, Melam says you can “Compost the pumpkin and save your favorite flowers.”.

    Shop Thanksgiving Decor Essentials:.

    Kristin Davis’s centerpiece is appealing due to its simplicity; not everything needs to be super showy and over the top to steal the show at the Thanksgiving table.

    💡 Key Takeaways

Buy these gifts for yourself, stuff your own stocking, use ‘em to drop some very unsubtle hints on your partner’s phone, or forward this list straight to your friends and family.     #44409. Eight Sleep’s Alexandra Zatarain on women-centered tech, the science of better sleep, and planning a career around motherhood

    Eight Sleep’s Alexandra Zatarain on women-centered tech, the science of better sleep, and planning a career around motherhood

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1464 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that this article is sponsored by Eight Sleep.
    • Alexandra Zatarain helped build Eight Sleep into a tech unicorn, and she’s expecting her first child in January.
    • According to recent reports, meet the expert: Alexandra Zatarain is the co-founder and VP of brand and marketing at Eight Sleep, the sleep-technology company behind the Pod.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that this article is sponsored by Eight Sleep. Thank you for supporting the brands that support Motherly and mamas.

    Alexandra Zatarain helped build Eight Sleep into a tech unicorn, and she’s expecting her first child in January. Going through pregnancy while running a global company has reshaped how she sees her own body, her industry and the product she’s building. On this episode of The Motherly Podcast, the co-founder of the sleep-technology company talks about the research that revealed Eight Sleep’s technology was improving men’s sleep more than women’s and what the company did about it, why sleep is the most notable thing women can protect, and the career advice she wishes more women heard before becoming mothers.

    According to recent reports, meet the expert: Alexandra Zatarain is the co-founder and VP of brand and marketing at Eight Sleep, the sleep-technology company behind the Pod. The Pod is an intelligent mattress cover that cools or heats each side to your ideal temperature automatically, maximizing deep sleep and minimizing wake-ups. A marketer and brand builder, she grew Eight Sleep from launch into a tech unicorn and helped create what the company calls the sleep fitness movement. Eight Sleep now sells in 37 countries. She’s expecting her first child in January with her husband, Matteo, the company’s co-founder and CEO.

    It has been revealed that alexandra Zatarain: So many things. I just turned 37, and I’ve seen so many friends go through pregnancy before me. After my first trimester, I felt so bad, thinking, what a terrible friend I was. When you haven’t experienced it, you have such little empathy for what a woman’s body is going through, especially when life keeps demanding so much of you and it doesn’t stop. I really didn’t understand that you could feel so different in your body for so long. It’s built so much more admiration for women and what we go through, and it’s let me embrace a feminine side of myself that in tech you usually don’t get to bring out.

    Recent findings suggest that alexandra Zatarain: It’s made me realize that the only way the world out there is going to change for our benefit as women and mothers is if more of us are the ones making the decisions. I just don’t see any way around it. We have a lot of parents at Eight Sleep, every executive on our team is a parent, but as a woman the experience is completely different. Unless we can share that first-hand knowledge, it’s going to be hard to make progress as fast as we need to. It’s unfortunate that it takes the first-person experience to become that advocate, because everyone should appreciate what mothers go through, given that we all come from a mother.

    Recent findings suggest that alexandra Zatarain: A couple of years ago, our clinical team, which is more than 90% women, was analyzing data from our user base and noticed our technology had been improving men’s sleep more than women’s. They asked, what are we missing in how we design this? It turned out the algorithms that manage temperature while you sleep had been fed more data representing men than women. That’s a classic problem in science, where women are underrepresented because our bodies are more complex. You have to account for where someone is in their hormonal journey, pregnancy, postpartum, perimenopause. So we invested a couple million dollars into research and developed features from it. That changed how we think about ourselves, less about helping everyone in a broad way and more about solving specific problems women have had for ages.

    Alexandra Zatarain: Sleep is the most crucial pillar of health. You would die sooner from sleep deprivation than from food deprivation, which tells you how fundamental it is. For women it matters even more because our hormones rule our lives, and sleep is the one tool we have to regulate them. If you sleep well, your chances of better hormonal balance go up significantly. It’s the best medicine we have, more than working out, more than any meal. The challenge is that those same hormones are often playing against us, making it harder to sleep well in different seasons of life, so keeping our routines as stable as possible helps counter what our bodies are going through.

    According to recent reports, alexandra Zatarain: The mindset piece is really notable. There’s so much going on, the anxiety, the intrusive thoughts, so not being too hard on yourself is the first step. Understanding that the season will pass should put you a little more at ease, because it’s not going to be your life forever. The other piece is setting yourself up with the right systems, and the most important one is available to everyone for free, which is routine. It helps your body a lot. When you do need to sleep, it’ll be easier for your body to fall asleep because it’s used to the schedule.

    Industry observers note that alexandra Zatarain: I’m very rigid about my sleep schedule. I travel a lot, so sleep is number one for me. I make space for eight to nine hours every night, and I’m pretty good at hitting it. I go to bed by 9:30 or 10 every single night no matter where I am in the world, and I don’t really use an alarm unless I have to wake up before 6, because my body just wakes up on its own. That schedule is the thing that’s changed my life the most. Second to that is the environment, the temperature in my room and my bed, the lights going dark, no noise.

    It has been revealed that alexandra Zatarain: I think of myself as an athlete, and we’re all sort of athletes in a way. My sport is making decisions about how to build this business, and that means I have to train, stay healthy and think long term. It’s not a sprint. We’ve been doing this for 12 years, so the question is how do I not burn out and stay here 20 or 30 years more. I’m also lucky I built this with my husband, so there’s no real line between business and personal life for us. It’s all mixed in, but it’s so purpose-driven that achieving that purpose every day is what feeds the energy.

    Alexandra Zatarain: I’m very open with them about how intentional I was. I did my embryo freezing in my early 30s because of where I was in life. And I tell them that if they want a career after they have a family, the best time to build equity in that career is to push as hard as you can before. Know what you want, because time isn’t always on our side as women. Move up the ranks, so that by the time you have kids you have more flexibility and maybe a higher income. It is possible, but it takes planning, it will require compromises, and very importantly it will require the right partner.

    Alexandra Zatarain: It starts with the people around you understanding what you truly need. Sometimes it’s as simple as the encouragement of, yes, go take a nap, yes, your body’s going through a lot. It gets harder once the baby’s home and the mom is maybe exclusively breastfeeding, because it really all falls on you. So have a plan in place ahead of time for how the load is going to be shared. Our partners are much more involved than previous generations, so have those conversations early. It doesn’t end with the birth plan. That’s where everything starts.

    It has been revealed that alexandra Zatarain: The first trimester was difficult, a lot of nausea, and it was very hard to function at the level I’m used to. I almost never get sick, so feeling sick every day was a huge shift. It put me in the trajectory to build the team that would make it possible for me to become a mother, to figure out what to delegate and who to elevate, and I’ve built a stronger team as a result. But the biggest thing is that it’s taught me to let go. I can’t control how I feel every day. As a Type A person I always want to be in control, and this has been like therapy, learning that I’m not in control of my body. I’m building a human, and it’s fine if for this season things just work differently.
